en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa,
and to Nara, the best of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī.
Then one should recite the victory hymn,
which issued from the lips of Dvaipāyana; it is immeasurable,
meritorious, purifying, a destroyer of sins, and auspicious.
For one who attains the Bhārata while it is being recited,
what need is there for consecration with the waters of Puṣkara?
Salutations to the teacher Vyāsa!
Salutations to you, O omniscient great seer,
son of Parāśara, the peaceful one;
salutations to you, O Nārāyaṇa.
They approached with affection to see the son of King Pārīkṣita, who had been consecrated.
The great ṛṣis, headed by Śaunaka,
having arrived, that royal sage honored them with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and other rites.
Having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, he brought joy to those who were seated comfortably at rest by means of their conversation.
Then Śatānīka asked about the supreme narrative of Nārāyaṇa,
relying upon whom he is the Lord of the World.
My ancestors,
those best of men, recovered their kingdom which had been seized by their enemies.
By me, my grandfather Parīkṣit was granted union with life by the God of gods.
I have heard the majesty of that god many times; who is capable of praising that Unborn One?
He within whose belly this entire universe, with its moving and non-moving beings,
rests; he from whose wrath Rudra was born.
And by the grace of that God, who is able to describe the full extent of his manifestations? Even the Grandfather (Brahmā) [is unable].
Therefore, O Lord, I desire to hear about the means of propitiating that All-Self, the Sovereign.
By what means, whether by mantras, secret doctrines, or ritual service, might I cross over the ocean of existence?
Whether by gifts, vows, fasts, recitations, or even by burnt offerings,
he is propitiated by all.
Hari is the remover of the afflictions; he can be propitiated—
tell us that, O best of beings.
That is the knowledge of all knowledges; that is the learning of all that has been heard;
that is the secret of all secrets.
That by which Viṣṇu is pleased is the supreme mantra among mantras,
and that is the great vow among vows.
That indeed is the best fast by which Keśava is pleased;
that is the true tongue which praises Hari.
That mind alone is praiseworthy which is offered to Him;
those two hands alone are praiseworthy which perform His worship.
That very body is a truly noble birth throughout all future lives,
which indeed manifests with horripilation.
From the failure to chant the names of Viṣṇu, there arises that loss, that great defect,
and that state of being blind, dull-witted, and mute.
If for even a moment or an instant Vāsudeva is not meditated upon,
that [moment] is surely a lotus-root in one's throat.
Or rather,
it is a disease of the uvula; indeed, that is not a tongue which does not speak the virtues of Hari.
In the same way, there are many snares;
even the ears of those with little intelligence, having bestowed their attention upon sound, [become ensnared].
Even without praise from Hari,
that single act of a person’s endeavor in this birth is not fruitless.
For those rushing toward the further shore, whatever action is performed with Govinda as its refuge,
a single prostration to Kṛṣṇa alone [is sufficient].
Meru, composed of all jewels, is the guide to the shore of liberation;
the sky is composed of all wonders.
The Gaṅgā embodies all sacred fords; Hari embodies all gods;
likewise, enjoyment possesses such qualities as these.
I have heard him many times being sung of by the Siddhas and others; therefore, O God, I desire to see that deity.
In order to propitiate Nārāyaṇa, the Lord who dwells within the hearts of the entire world, Vdha_001.023–001.024.
O best of sages, today that which is infinite, of immeasurable splendor, the benefactor of the world, and the vital breath of the universe— that [I shall describe] to you.
Having heard these words of him who desired to win his favor and was worthy of showing grace, [he replied].
All those sages attained supreme satisfaction from Hari, who was bearing their devotion.
And all those best of sages [spoke] to Śaunaka, the best of the Bhṛgus,
according to the truth, saying, "O Blessed One, to him..."
"Let it be told," they urged.
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, you are a vast treasury of all knowledge in this matter."
O ascetic rich in austerity, you are a lamp in the darkness!
Thus addressed by the best of sages with affection for that king, [he spoke].
Then, out of devotion for the God of gods,
the illustrious Lord, being thus addressed, replied with a gentle voice.
O protector of the earth, as for what you ask me, Śaunaka, regarding the propitiation of Kṛṣṇa toward that lord of the earth—
Therefore, listen here with a one-pointed mind: the beginningless, supreme Brahman,
which pervades all beings.
He stands beyond both the existent and the non-existent, beyond primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa), from whom the agitation of the two invincible principles proceeds.
Because those two Great Souls, who are eternal and all-pervading, were the agitators at the beginning of the world, [the universe was called] the Brahmāṇḍa.
The stainless one is the cause of creation;
yet, though being without cause, the Supreme Lord, the Self of all, is born.
And he attains the state of Pradhāna and Puruṣa; thereafter, as a lord, he assumes the state of Brahmā at his own will.
Then, as the Lord of the World, he remains as Viṣṇu to protect the universe, and as Rudra at its dissolution.
The Imperishable One acts according to His own will;
He is that one syllable, the supreme abode, the Great Reality beyond both being and non-being.
Having prostrated before the Supreme State,
I shall proclaim that which was previously told to me by my father.
It is said that his father told this to him, and Uśanas told it to him; he,
in turn, having propitiated Bhṛgu, [taught it].
The propitiation of Hari was obtained from Brahmā, and it was also obtained by the high-souled Bhṛgu.
And in ancient times,
this supreme [teaching] was obtained from the presence of the Lord by the great seers, including Marīci.
When the Lord Brahmā, whose birth is manifest, was the master of the great seers, he spoke of the supreme yoga.
Then the Blessed One, Brahmā, the Lord of the World, having prostrated himself, was indeed addressed by all the great sages.
The yoga for the welfare of all beings which was taught by you has its source in the Self;
yet it can be attained by many.
O Lord of the world, sense objects are difficult for men to conquer throughout their births, O Master, for they drag the senses away.
The fluctuations of the mind are fickle and exceedingly difficult to restrain;
how then can passion and the like be conquered?
For even in hundreds of years,
the mind cannot become fit for yoga if these [senses] have not been conquered.
O Brahmin, these men are short-lived even in the Kṛta age,
as well as in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages.
How much more so now that the Kali age has arrived?
O Blessed One, you who know the means, being well-disposed toward us, you ought to speak.
By which means men submerged in the waters of suffering may cross over this ocean of existence without effort.
Having obtained the great boat that is Brahman,
they cross over the ocean of existence;
reflect upon this accordingly.
Thus addressed, Brahmā then explained the yoga of action (kriyāyoga) to those high-souled sages.
Out of a desire for the welfare of men,
worship Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Universe, without weariness.
[They served] that unborn Lord of the world day and night with various forms of service, vows, and fasts.
And by means of the satiation of the Brahmins with various desired objects that grant satisfaction to the mind.
Worship Keśava; be devoted to him, fix your minds upon him, perform actions for his sake, and take refuge in him.
Those whose vision is fixed on Him and whose minds are absorbed in Him perceive Him as existing in everything; thus, all their actions are performed for Him alone.
In that regard, renounce everything within yourselves by means of the self; He shall be your doer.
This is that Imperishable Brahman.
From whom, in whom, and in what manner both Pradhāna and Puruṣa abide, they both being all-pervasive.
He who is beyond all that is beyond, the supreme,
he alone is the Puruṣottama, from whom all this undivided universe proceeds.
Having propitiated that Lord of the World, the unmanifest cause of liberation, whether it be that which moves or that which does not move.
"Having heard from Brahmā that it is inconceivable, without grasping, and that one is liberated through the yoga of action," Vdha_001.057–Vdha_001.058.
O best of sages, for the benefit of mankind, they composed treatises on yoga as a secret doctrine.
Having performed manifold acts of liberation,
he worships Hṛṣīkeśa, the Supreme Self and Lord of the World.
O tiger among kings, I shall [recite] those [verses] which remove all sins, belonging to the Lord of All and the Creator of All.
I shall speak of another supreme secret; let it be heard by those who desire to cross over from that [suffering].
Since there is nothing whatsoever that serves as a supreme refuge for those within [this world], even in the slightest degree, other than the boat of Viṣṇu.
While rising, think of Hari; while walking, think of Keśava;
while eating, think of Govinda.
While sleeping, think of Mādhava;
thus, with a one-pointed mind,
you have taken refuge in Madhusūdana.
You shall cross the waters of saṃsāra—
the infinite, praiseworthy, ancient Person,
the unborn creator of the world who is himself uncreated.
For those who have taken refuge in Hari, the Lord,
and who partake in liberation, there is indeed no further rebirth;
listen, O tiger among the Kurus!
This is the unsurpassed dialogue between the royal sage Ambarīṣa and the divine Wielder of the Discus.
King Ambarīṣa,
while protecting the earth,
was indeed anxious about reaching the end of the pairs of opposites.
Desiring [this], that bull among men,
desiring the destruction of the pairs of opposites from Govinda, the God of gods—
Subsisting on no food, he performed austerities while reciting the eternal Brahman;
after a long time had passed for him—
As he bore supreme devotion, Lord Viṣṇu, the sovereign and lord of all the worlds, was pleased.
Assuming the form of Indra and moving with the gait of a lordly elephant, he then spoke to that lord of the earth.
O royal sage, tell me what task is established in your mind;
I have arrived as a granter of boons.
"Choose a boon, O you of noble vows.
Having been addressed thus, the king then looked toward Purandara.
Raising up the guest-offering (arghya), he replied:
"Welcome to you, O Lord! I am not worshipping you."
This salutation with joined palms is offered by me to you;
you are the giver of boons to those who seek boons— grant us our desired boons.
"O King, penance is performed by you and others for the sake of obtaining boons;
for what purpose, then, do you [seek one] from us?"
You do not grant what is desired;
O Lord of Gods, this effort of mine is not for the sake of a boon from you.
Know that I have undertaken this effort for the sake of propitiating Viṣṇu;
for I belong to all the gods.
Likewise, the lords of the three worlds,
as well as the gods beginning with Āditya, always carry out my command alone.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras,
the two Nāsatyas, the hosts of Maruts, the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), and the Sādhyas.
The Viśvedevas and the great sages carry out my very command;
for who else besides me is the bestower of boons?
Accept what you desire;
you are indeed Indra, the god who is truly the lord of the three worlds.
You too have attained sovereignty; therefore, I shall gratify him,
for the three worlds are yours, O Lord of Gods.
I propitiate that Lord, under whose control the seven worlds lie within his belly, O Great-Souled One.
O Lord of the Gods, you whose body we have attained and who indeed abide within us, are united with all the immortals.
I bow to that Janārdana,
whose night is the closing of Brahmā’s eyes and whose day is his opening of the eyes.
I bow down to that Janārdana, the worshipful Lord, the undecaying one,
who is the God that withdraws the world.
I propitiate that Viṣṇu, who is the creator and the protector of this triad, and who is its source.
Formerly, Hiraṇyakaśipu and your enemy Hiraṇyākṣa were [slain] by him through compassion for you.
The two Daityas have been slain; I bow to Him by whom,
O Śakra, that which was formerly taken away by the powerful one was restored to you.
Having bound him, the sovereignty over the three worlds,
I bow to that Janārdana;
be gracious, O Śakra, and depart.
I too am established here,
performing austerities in order to behold Nārāyaṇa Hari, the Lord of the World.
Having been addressed thus by him,
Janārdana, in the form of Śakra,
spoke to him again out of anger.
O King, established in asceticism,
if by my word you do not abandon your penance today—
I shall strike you with my vajra; wake up if you so desire!
Your offense is not even slight.
O Lord of the Thirty-three,
even so, if you consider me worthy of death, then hurl your weapon.
It is indeed heard that for men who bear devotion toward Govinda,
the gods become their adversaries.
"I am an ascetic; where is my freedom from attachment, and where is such anger as yours?
This has been understood, O Govinda."
Many obstacles arise for a man who is intent on the highest good, and no other good is found [that can withstand them].
Therefore, O Purandara, strike me or do not strike me with your thunderbolt;
I shall never abandon Govinda.
"I worship another,
O sir; neither Vajra nor the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra), nor you, nor any other gods or asuras."
They are capable of slaying even Īśāna when Janārdana resides in the heart;
moreover, what is the use of saying more?
I shall not speak further than this;
do as you desire, and I will do what you wish.
Having spoken thus to the lord of the gods,
that king again practiced asceticism, observing a vow of silence.
But Keśava was not satisfied by that;
then Kaiṭabhārdana revealed his own true form.
Four-armed, with noble limbs, clearly wearing a crown and a garland; Airāvata and Garuḍa [are his mounts].
At that very moment,
that excellent king beheld the Lord Acyuta, clad in yellow garments.
Having beheld him with his head bowed in devotion, he suddenly went down to the earth;
and the protector of the land replied:
Having prostrated with palms joined in reverence,
his body covered in horripilation, he then praised Padmanābha with this hymn.
Victory to you, O primordial God, unconquerable! Victory to you, the creator of the world’s manifestation!
Victory to you of vast form, the imperishable!
Victory to you, the omnipresent and inconceivable! Victory to you, the remover of birth and old age! Victory to you, the all-pervading! Victory to you, the indivisible!
Victory to you, O Lord, who reside within all beings! Victory to you, O Master of Sacrifice! Victory to you, whose doctrines are fully realized!
O Keśava, who deludes by means of illusion; O sinless one, for the sake of maintaining the world; O Boar, conqueror of the earth, victory to you!
Victory to you, O Nṛsiṃha, enemy of the enemies of the gods; O Vāmana, destroyer of the distress of the gods who are terrified by their foes!
Victory to you who have traversed the entire earth!
O Lord of the worlds, victory is yours! Victory is yours, O Giver of all, O All-pervading One!
Victory is yours, O Lord of all beings;
salutations be unto you, who are the object of meditation for yogis. Salutations be unto the one who is indefinable.
Salutations to you whose nature is subtle;
salutations to you, the triple-formed one;
O you whose form is the universe, let there be salutations to you.
That form which is meditated upon by Brahmā and the others,
which is beyond both being and non-being,
and which cannot be distinguished by specific attributes; to that [I bow].
Salutations again and again to you;
from that [state] arises the form called Puruṣa,
which is beyond qualities (nirguṇa) yet the enjoyer of qualities (guṇabhoktṛ).
I bow to that subtle one who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), O Hari; to you,
the most subtle and yet the Great One.
That form of yours is natural;
O God, I bow to you who exist through various kinds of forms.
Your worldly activity is performed with ease;
salutations to You, the Self of the gods. Be gracious, O Viṣṇu, O Govinda!
O Vāsudeva, O Maheśvara! Thus praised, Keśava, the Lord of the World, spoke as follows.
Making the world resound with his voice, he said to Ambarīṣa, the lord of the earth:
"Ambarīṣa, I am pleased."
"O sinless one, through your devotion and this hymn of praise, choose a boon, O knower of dharma, whatever dwells in your mind."
This alone is a praiseworthy boon, O Lord of the World, that you have been seen;
for the sight of you is not for those devoid of merit.
O Lord, O Acyuta, this devotion of mine toward you, which has existed from my childhood, is indeed difficult to find even in dreams.
The Blessed One alone, who dwells in the hearts of all embodied beings, knows that; O Lord, it is through Your grace that I know it as well.
He enjoys unimpeded sovereignty on earth, as well as an exceedingly great treasury and army,
and the highest health of body.
"O women, due to the power of food and drink,
there is not even the slightest loss for me; my strength is that of a thousand elephants."
I maintain my lineage, O slayer of enemies; my servants are disciplined,
and my people are full of devotion.
And there would be a decline of dharma, O Lord of Gods;
for I have no desire for the protection of the earth.
Whatever I wish for, that very thing [I shall obtain].
"O Lord of the World, everything exists;
for I have realized that the Blessed One Govinda is indeed gracious."
Prosperities do not exist for one who is not serene;
likewise, O Keśava, even one who stands in the midst of all pleasures and delights [is not serene].
With a mind agitated by fear, O Keśava, if your mind is inclined toward grace toward me— Vdha_002.057 Vdha_002.057 Vdha_002.057.
Therefore, you ought to lift me up from this bottomless ocean of saṃsāra;
for those pleasures have no end.
That which is suffering is not happiness; that which results in future suffering is like the eating of the *kiṃpāka* fruit.
O Teacher,
O Janārdana of the worlds,
show favor by granting me that gift of knowledge through which—
When he said, "Let us cross over the snare," Govinda,
the knower of yoga, spoke to him.
When the seedless yoga (*nirbīja-yoga*) had been taught in its entirety,
the king then prostrated before Acyuta.
Again the mighty-armed one, standing bowed in humility, said:
"O God of gods, yoga has been taught by you."
"O Madhusūdana, that which has been described by you cannot be attained by me, nor by other men whose senses are unsubdued."
Objects of the senses are always difficult for men to conquer,
as they constantly attract the senses; therefore,
one should strive for mastery over the senses regarding them.
Who can overcome the mind, which is difficult to conquer and fickle, and which proclaims "I" and "mine" among those who are powerful?
"How can passion and the other afflictions be conquered even over the course of many lifetimes?
O Lord of Gods, this is what I desire."
Through your grace, with my impurities destroyed and passion and the other afflictions unsubdued, may I attain immortality.
If you are thus desirous of liberation,
O Lord of Men, then listen to that *kriyāyoga* which pertains to all [beings].
It brings about the destruction of the afflictions. Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, and bow down to me.
Thus, by practicing yoga with your self thus directed toward me, you shall come to me alone—
meditating on me and sacrificing to me.
My devotees, who are intent upon me,
devoted to my worship, and dedicated to my service— such men attain dissolution in me.
Behold me, the Lord, established equally in all beings; with whom can you have enmity? You are the creator.
In this way, once you have known me— the Self— both in all that moves and that which is stationary, you shall abandon these defects.
O King, if the mind, because of its fickleness, does not find rest in me, the state of having accomplished all that was to be done will surely come to pass.
Fashion a body in my likeness;
you shall worship it with various costly offerings made of gold, silver, and other precious materials.
And worship her, O King, having fixed your mind upon her;
abandon all other refuges.
She alone has been worshipped by you with devotion and meditated upon as your benefactress,
whether you were walking, standing, sleeping, or eating.
Meditating thus upon that very [Self]— first in front and behind,
above and below, as well as on the sides— he likewise contemplates it within himself.
With baths using the delightful waters of sacred fords, with garments, ornaments, and edible foods,
and with captivating songs and instrumental music.
O best of men, bowing with devotion, you should offer her whatever food and other things are desired by the king.
"Delight in the hymn of praise offered by me; if my heart is drawn by passion toward the Gandharvas," [then let it be so].
Having focused your intellect upon me, sing that story of mine;
for the mind finds delight in that narrative.
If my meditation on that is to be heard by you with a heart full of devotion,
[then listen to] the accounts of the incarnations.
O King, those mental supports which have their minds thus fixed upon me must all be abandoned.
Do not fear; you shall abandon [them].
Even though your passion and hatred are not yet exhausted, you shall be supremely devoted to my service.
"You shall attain that state; do not fear. Fix your mind on me, having surrendered everything to me."
Whatever you possess, including yourself, perform those actions for my sake; do not transgress the dharma.
Rule the kingdom, O best of men,
having offered the earth to me; and those who are intent on obstructing that [act]— [subdue them].
O Lord of the Earth,
having established yourself in the yoga of action, I have explained all of that to you. Vdha_002.082–083.
Fix your mind on me;
O Lord of the World,
for my sake, take refuge in the yoga of action dedicated to me.
Relate this in detail;
for you are gracious and the destroyer of suffering,
and indeed there is none but you who can speak for us.
O Teacher of the World, you alone are capable; please be gracious to me and explain this secret and purifying matter.
"By my grace, your domestic priest Vasiṣṭha will relate all of this to you in its entirety."
"And he shall know it in its entirety," having said this, the Lord Hari, the sovereign of all worlds, vanished.
And that king returned once more from the forest to his own city;
having been established in his kingdom, the protector of the earth—
Having prostrated before his family priest Vasiṣṭha, he questioned him regarding the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
O Blessed One, you have been commanded by the Great-Souled God of Gods regarding everything concerning the yoga of action.
"You shall indeed explain it.
"Therefore, I ask you everything regarding Keśava through the yoga of action."
Tell me how I may be able to satisfy Īśāna;
by the grace of the God, [may all my desires be fulfilled].
Memory has also come to me;
I shall tell you this entire knowledge— understand it.
The son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Daitya, possessed great wisdom and became devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
He questioned Śukra, the best of the Bhṛgus and his own domestic priest: "O Blessed One, [tell me] of the form of Nṛsiṃha..."
O dear one, as Viṣṇu was desiring to slay him,
I beheld within his body the entire triple world, beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvas.
Brahmā Prajāpati, Indra, Paśupati together with the Rudras,
the eight Vasus, and likewise the Ādityas.
The earth, the twelve-day period,
the nights, the quarters, the sky, the multitude of stars,
the two Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Sādhyas— Vdha_003.007–008.
The Viśvedevas as well as the ṛṣis,
the rain-mountains as well as the rivers,
and the seven primary mountain ranges.
The seven oceans, the seasons, the wildernesses, and the forests,
as well as the entire surface of the earth, were all brought together.
Whatever else was seen by me upon his body— both this and that—
I [saw] him, the undecaying God.
"O Blessed One, I wish to propitiate you with your permission;
if I am worthy of your favor."
Thinking, "This man is devoted to me," you should now instruct me in that great means of propitiating Hari.
O Lord of the Daityas, you are surely worthy of being favored by the God whose birth is unmanifest, for the sake of his propitiation.
If that mind of yours is inclined toward him, and if you wish to propitiate Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods.
O Asura, become a devotee of the Blessed One who is without beginning or end; for Viṣṇu is not [attained] by those who are not devotees of the Blessed One.
It is not possible for mortals to truly know, praise, or even behold Him;
how much less, indeed, can they enter?
Purified through many births, those men whose minds are fixed upon Him indeed become Bhāgavatas.
They enter Viṣṇu; however,
as long as the accumulation of their sins has not been exhausted, men are born again.
A mind directed toward Govinda develops aversion toward Govinda;
it censures the twice-born and the Vedas.
The man who would recognize that [truth] finds delight in heretical sects; such a delight in men arises from the waters of Viṣṇu’s Māyā.
When the destruction of the sins of fallen and evil-minded men occurs,
then [they are restored] among the Vedas and the twice-born.
And when only a very small portion remains, you will have such faith in Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sacrifice.
O Lord of the Daityas, those men whose accumulation of sin has ceased become Bhāgavatas at that time.
For men wandering here in this cycle of existence, which is difficult to traverse due to their karma,
he alone is indeed the hand to hold.
Janārdana is pleased by devotion; therefore,
having become a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata),
[worship] Hari, who removes all sins.
Propitiate him with supreme devotion;
Keśava will be pleased. What are the characteristics of the Bhāgavatas?
O Guru, what qualities do men possess,
and what is to be performed by the devotees of the Lord?
Tell me that, O Bhārgava.
He who does not harm living beings by deed, thought, or word,
and who is devoted in spirit to Govinda;
O Daitya,
he indeed is a devotee of the Blessed One who always honors and approves of both the Brahmins and the Vedas.
O Daitya, he who does not seek to harm another in debate is indeed a devotee of the Lord;
for he knows Hari to be all the gods.
O Daitya, he regards all worlds as Keśava and does not consider himself to be other than them; for he is a true Bhāgavata.
Whether it be a god, a human, or another being; whether the earth, water, sky, or the directions; or even the self, O lords of gods—
Know that man who worships none other than Janārdana to be indeed a Bhāgavata.
He who truly understands that everything which has come to be and exists within phenomenal existence is the very nature of the Blessed One— Vdha_003.030.
But that man who is a devotee of the Lord,
being permeated by a spirit of devotion, removes the fear of worldly existence.
He who possesses the state of being "Bhagavān" is a man devoted to the Lord (bhāgavata); however,
he who does not cultivate that state [is not].
That man who commits no evil toward any living being through deed, thought,
or word is a devotee of the Blessed One.
He who, independent of external objects, performs the ritual service of the Blessed One with devotion, accomplishes it through his inner disposition.
He should be known as a devotee of the Lord for whom there are no enemies,
no friends,
and no neutral persons, nor any worldly inclinations.
For he who sees all this as Viṣṇu is indeed a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata),
having performed intense penance in this world.
Men do not attain through sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees that same goal which the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) have attained.
O performer of sacrifice, Śatakratu, the king of the gods, is being looked upon from nearby by the devotees of the Lord who have fallen from yoga.
How much more so those who have reached the further shore of yoga?
The Vedas exist for the accomplishment of sacrifice,

in every way, they are a great divinity.
Therefore, with every effort, [one should honor them].
One should protect Brāhmaṇas in times of distress;
for even Śakra, the lord of the gods, fears the foremost of the twice-born.
"The gods praise generosity"— thus those who know the Dharma understand;
therefore, [one should learn] the various rules for giving.
Listen with a well-composed mind:
the gift of gold, the gift of cows,
and likewise the gift of earth.
These indeed are the purifiers; they deliver one to the hereafter,
whatever is most dear to one in this world.
Whatever is most beloved in the home should be given to one who possesses virtue by him who desires that very thing to become inexhaustible.
By bestowing the gift of gold, the gift of cows,
and indeed the gift of the earth, one truly gives these.
One is liberated from all sins by that which you give to distinguished persons and that which you eat day after day.
I consider that wealth of yours to be [mere] knowledge; you are merely guarding the remainder for someone else.
The names are identical, yet they are praised as distinct.
O Indra among kings, these three, which yield equal fruits, should always be given:
cows, land, and sacred knowledge.
In the same way, O slayer of enemies, by giving water, one obtains satisfaction through the name of that which yields a corresponding fruit.
Whatever object is intended by one's resolve is given to the Brahmins, who are indeed seekers for the sake of wealth.
By that [merit], one becomes wise;
however, he who does not give to a petitioner, especially to a preeminent twice-born, sinks low.
When this purpose is present, the evil-minded man [offers] cows and oxen,
as well as an umbrella, clothing, and sandals.
Drink and likewise food should be given to those who ask;
thus is charity prescribed.
The supreme star is the radiant one;
this sacrifice has been ordained for you, purified by faith and accompanied by sacrificial fees.
And he is distinguished among sacrifices; this is the path established by those who know the rules of giving, who give without malice.
By means of those gifts, purified by faith, which the wise offer to the best of the twice-born, they shall satisfy [the ancestors] and go to that [state].
For just as a farmer reaps fruit from a well-tilled field, even so does one who gives to the Brāhmaṇas.
The giver enjoys the fruit; and indeed,
there exist Brāhmaṇas who are truthful and deeply learned in the Vedas.
And he does not give gifts;
his acquisition of wealth is in vain.
Rising again and again, one must remain vigilant.
What good deed have I performed today— whether it be a gift given, or a gift caused to be given, or even an act of encouragement?
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should give repeatedly as it arises to the Brāhmaṇas,
for a worthy recipient will come.
That vessel shall deliver [the donor]:
both the vessel consisting of the Vedas and the vessel consisting of austerity.
That vessel which is unmixed shall deliver [one];
I shall now declare the chapter on austerity.
Listen as I declare this to you:
there is indeed nothing superior to austerity;
through austerity one obtains the fruit.
The sages, having applied themselves to austerity,
rejoice together with the deities; through austerity, heaven is attained.
Through austerity, fame is attained;
through austerity, a man obtains longevity and enjoyments.
Knowledge, discernment, faith,
good fortune, and supreme beauty—
all this is obtained through austerity.
Whatever one desires with the mind,
those who have not performed austerities never attain the world of Brahmā.
Whatever purpose a person undertakes when performing austerity,
he attains all of that.

In the next world and in this one as well, a man who drinks liquor, one who commits adultery with another's wife, a killer of an embryo, and one who violates the bed of his teacher— Vdha_054.005–054.006.
Through austerity one overcomes everything and is liberated from all things—
even Sthāṇu, the Lord of All.
And Viṣṇu himself, the eternal, as well as Brahmā, Agni, and Śakra—
these eternal ones perform austerities.
The sages who have sublimated their vital energy rejoice in heaven through their austerity,
assembled together with the deities.
Through austerity, sovereignty is attained; Śakra, the lord of all the gods,
protects everything through austerity.
Day after day, the slayer of Vṛtra [protects] the two gods, the Sun and the Moon,
who are devoted to the welfare of the entire world.
By austerity alone do the constellations and the planets shine;
there is no such happiness in the world.
Those who know the Dharma understand that indeed there is no happiness whatsoever without austerity; it is through austerity alone that all happiness is attained.
And Viśvāmitra attained the status of a Brahmin through austerity; indeed,
everything is achieved through austerity.
And he enjoys every happiness who practices austerities in the forest,
a sage subsisting on roots and fruits.
Even by reciting a single verse,
one goes to the supreme goal;
therefore, having undertaken austerity, [one should do so].
One should pray for whatever is desired.
Truth alone is the supreme Brahman;
truth alone is the supreme austerity.
Truth alone is the supreme sacrifice; truth alone is the supreme sacred revelation;
truth remains awake among the gods.
Liberation is the fruit of the tree of truth;
it is austerity, fame, merit,
the primordial ordinance, and knowledge.
Everything is established in truth; truth is the sacrifice, as well as the Vedas,
the mantras, and the goddess Sarasvatī.
Likewise, the practice of vows, truth, the syllable Om, and truth itself— by means of truth, the wind moves.
By truth the sun shines;
by truth the fire burns;
by truth one goes to heaven.
By means of truth, Parjanya casts down water upon the surface of the earth;
it is the completion of all the Vedas.
For one who speaks the truth in this world,
that shall be equal to a thousand horse-sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
Truth was weighed against [all else] on a scale;
indeed, this truth excels a thousand horse-sacrifices.
The sages are devoted to truth;
the sages possess the prowess of truth;
the sages have truth as their path.
Those who have gone from here to the supreme perfection— by truth the gods are pleased,
as are the ancestors and the Brahmins.
They say truth is the supreme dharma;
therefore, one should not violate the truth.
The sages are devoted to truth.
Therefore, truth is superior;
those devoted to truth always rejoice in heaven like the gods.
They approach by means of celestial chariots;
for truth must always be spoken,
for there is nothing superior to truth.
Whoever should perform this measure of worship shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices in that fathomless, stainless, and pure [state].
Those endowed with mental discipline should bathe in the auspicious lake at the ford of Truth;
that is remembered as the supreme bath.
O King, those who do not speak untruth for their own sake, for the sake of others, or even for the sake of their sons—
Those men go to heaven,
O Yudhiṣṭhira; moreover, this was sung of old by those who know the Dharma.
The man who speaks the truth and does not utter falsehood,
having reached the worlds free from passion, [remains there].
Having dwelt there for eternal years,
he is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous as one of great intelligence.
One should be disciplined and devoted to yoga.
The sun and the moon, fire and wind,
heaven, earth, water, the heart, and Yama— [these are the witnesses].
Day and night, as well as both twilights, and Dharma itself know the conduct of a man;
therefore, the virtuous must never speak untruth.
Those who know the Dharma speak thus:
one who speaks the truth, blazing with splendor,
is not deprived of virtue, fame, wealth, or desire.
This is indeed the Dharma established by Vāṇī; it is the Vedic Dharma according to the determination of Dharma,
and thus it is in accordance with what is right.
That which has been proclaimed in the chapter on Truth— the wise man should take that as his authority;
there is nothing higher than Truth.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, I shall proclaim for all the social classes those [rites] that must be observed by those who have fasted.
O Pāṇḍava, learn now that fruit which is to be attained through fasting when it is performed according to the prescribed rules.
O King, he obtains his desires exactly as he wishes; these rites have been ordained by me, desiring your welfare.
For those humans whose minds are dedicated solely to me, fasting on both the fifth and the sixth lunar days [is meritorious].
O Pāṇḍava, by fasting on the full moon day, one becomes handsome, fortunate,
and indeed blessed.
O son of Kuntī, by fasting on the eighth and the fourteenth days of the bright fortnight, one becomes free from disease.
And he is born indeed endowed with vigor;
he who, during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, always eats but one meal a day.
O King, he shall share in the fruits of agriculture and be born with many sons,
O Indra among kings, during the month of Pauṣa.
He who passes [a day] with a single meal becomes fortunate, handsome,
and endowed with wisdom.
O tiger among men, he who passes the month of Māgha eating only one meal a day dedicated to the ancestors—
He who passes the month of Bhādrapada eating but one meal a day attains an infinite reward.
He becomes beloved by women, and they come under his control;
this applies to the month of Caitra, O tiger among men.
O tiger among men, he who passes a month eating but one meal a day and observes silence attains the fruit [of his merit].
He who passes the month of Bhagadaivata eating but one meal a day becomes beloved among women.
And those women become submissive to him,
O tiger among men, who passes the month of Caitra eating but a single meal a day.
O lord of men, he who passes the month of Vaiśākha by eating but one meal a day is born into a great family.
Whether a man or a woman,
one shall attain preeminence among kinsmen by fasting during the month of Jyeṣṭha when there is no water available.
O tiger among men, he who passes his time eating but a single meal per day becomes endowed with sovereignty and is born as one who possesses women.
O best of the Bharatas, he who passes the month of Āṣāḍha by eating only one meal a day becomes a hero and possesses abundant grain.
O tiger among men, he who passes the month of Śrāvaṇa with only a single meal will be born with many sons.
O King, in whichever state one may be reborn by observing the month of Bhādrapada, there one shall increase one's kinsmen.
He who passes his time eating but one meal a day becomes wealthy and heroic,
and attains sovereign power.
The man who passes the month of Āśvayuja eating but a single meal a day becomes wealthy and possessed of many vehicles.
A man who eats only once a day throughout the month of Kārttika will be born with many sons.
He is born brave, possessed of many wives, and endowed with fame— these,
O best of men, are the months.
O lord of men, listen now to those rules for the lunar days (tithis) that have been proclaimed regarding eating but a single meal.
The man who passes the fourth mealtime on every fortnight obtains abundant wealth.
The Blessed One Agni said:
"He who, month by month, should pass a single meal on every fourth [day],"
He becomes a sharer in agriculture, a sharer in fame,
and is also born as one possessed of splendor;
this occurs for three nights in every fortnight.
He who recites this in an assembly, a herd-station, a city, or a village, O bull among men,
attains greatness.
He who passes three nights every month subsisting on a single meal attains the leadership of the Gaṇas.
He who eats in the evening and likewise in the morning, and does not drink anything in between, [attains] a state free from rivals and free from thorns.
Constantly devoted to non-violence and offering oblations into the sacred fire,
he [attains his goal] in exactly six years.
It is accomplished; there is no doubt in this matter.
A human being obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O King, by observing an eighth meal [every day] for a year,
one attains the fruit of the Gavāmaya sacrifice.
The person attains the fruit; he travels by means of a celestial chariot for a full thousand years.
He is glorified in the heavenly world;
moreover, whether he be distressed or even afflicted by disease,
he who undertakes fasting shall go [there].
At every step, he obtains the fruit of a sacrifice by chanting my name;
he travels by means of a celestial chariot.
And a hundred apsarases shall delight that man here in a celestial chariot possessing the splendor of the sun.
Dwelling thus, he prospers in happiness; neither angry, nor diseased, nor afflicted,
he who undertakes fasting shall go [to the highest state].
Hear also what the fruit of that is:
he is honored in the heavenly world for a hundred thousand years.
Established in himself, with his resolve fulfilled,
happy and free from defilement,
he prospers in happiness within that radiant light.
O Bhārata, for as many pores as there are on his body,
for that many years he rejoices in the divine realms in heaven.
There is no scripture superior to the Veda; there is no teacher equal to a mother;
there is no gain superior to dharma.
There is no austerity superior to fasting;
there is nothing purifying in heaven or on earth greater than the Brahmins.
Indeed, no other austerity is known to be equal to fasts;
for by fasting according to the prescribed rules, the gods [attained their status].
The sages attained the third heaven and achieved supreme perfection through their fasts.
For a thousand divine years, the wise Viśvāmitra practiced patience by subsisting on a single meal each day.
By whom [this state] was attained:
Cyavana, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and Bhṛgu.
For all these, O Indra among kings, have attained heaven by this method— being patient and deeply learned.
Whoever recites or listens with devotion to that which has been proclaimed by me,
for that person no sin exists.
A man is liberated from all bodily afflictions and is no longer overcome by sins;
for the status of a Brahmin is exceedingly difficult to attain.
One becomes a Brāhmaṇa by birth,
or a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya; indeed, one is born as such by birth alone.
But by evil conduct, a man of wicked soul falls from his station,
even after having attained a superior station.
Therefore, a wise man should guard himself;
for he who, having abandoned the status of a Brahmin, devotes himself to the status of a Kshatriya [falls].
Fallen from the state of a Brāhmaṇa, he is born in a Kṣatriya womb,
or else he performs the duties of a Vaiśya.
One who performs the duties of a Śūdra is born from a Vaiśya womb;
performing the duties of a Śūdra,
one attains the state of a Śūdra.
Having fallen from that state and reached an evil destiny, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he entered the womb of a Śūdra.
If one does not practice the Dharma,
having fallen away from the human state, he is born in the womb of an animal.
Because of his practice of unrighteousness, the fool revolves right there;
therefore, having attained an auspicious state, he remains.
But through negligence,
a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires and performs sacrifices may perish within the belly [of a demon].
He shall partake of the destiny of a Śūdra; he attains the state of a Kṣatriya; he attains the state of a Vaiśya.
Having died after eating the food of such a person, that Brahmin attains that very womb;
having attained the auspicious status of a Brahmin, he is reborn there.
He who despises that which is difficult to obtain,
and does not know what may or may not be eaten—
that Kṣatriya shall become a twice-born man (a Brahmin).
I shall explain to you in its entirety that action by which an intelligent Śūdra is indeed reborn as a Vaiśya.
By which one may become of the highest caste;
having become a Śūdra, he should perform the duties of a Śūdra as they have been prescribed.
But he who, with an undisturbed mind, always performs service as is proper toward the three castes;
That Śūdra shall attain the status of a Vaiśya;
I shall now describe in due order how a Vaiśya likewise attains the status of a Kṣatriya.
Pure and a hater of sinful people,
he maintained the sacred fire and offered oblations according to the prescribed rule.
That Vaiśya is born into a Kṣatriya family; of this there is no doubt.
But a Kṣatriya is born from a Brahmin womb.
Listen to how that comes about:
he gives gifts and performs sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by the distribution of prescribed sacrificial fees.
Seeking heaven, he constantly studies;
he always maintains the three sacred fires as his refuge; and he is ever the giver of aid to those in distress.
Protecting his subjects with righteousness,
he approached his own wife according to the prescribed rule during her fertile period.
"Let hospitality be shown to all; let the three goals of life be pursued; let it be given and let it be enjoyed by the Śūdras and by beggars."
Speaking thus of eternal perfection,
for the sake of cows and Brahmins,
he was slain while facing the enemy in battle.
A Kṣatriya may become a Brāhmaṇa;
one who knows the ritual rules is born as a priest within a Kṣatriya family.
Those of all castes who abide on the path of the righteous attain an unimpaired heaven;
yet the state of a Brāhmaṇa is extremely difficult to attain.
It is attained by men only with great difficulty;
therefore, one should protect the supreme state of Brahmanahood with every effort.
Gold is the supreme gift; gold is the highest sacrificial fee;
this is the supreme purifier.
This is a great means of securing well-being;
it protects ten generations of ancestors and descendants,
as well as oneself.
Even after committing a hundred sins,
those who bestow gold upon Brahmins shall cause themselves to cross over [to liberation].
We have heard that all the deities bestow their gifts upon those men who possess a pure mind.
For Agni is all the deities, and gold is the consumer of oblations;
therefore, by one who gives gold—
And all the deities have been given; and in the absence of fire, they place gold in the positions of the sacrificial fires.
But those who, having kindled this fire,
should offer it at the rising of the sun with reference to a vow, [they attain the highest goal].
They shall obtain all desires;
the giver of gold enjoys his desired wishes in the heavenly world.
He wanders here and there, shining with his own radiant and resplendent splendor.
Carried by his own desire, that best of men, wafting divine fragrances, shall wander here and there in heaven.
Therefore, men on earth should give gold according to their own capacity;
for there is nothing higher than this in the world.
He who bestows pure gold as a gift attains immediate liberation from sin.
He is honored in the heavenly world for many thousands of years.
[This was said] by the one who formerly created the worlds.
Cows were created by the Self-Existent One for the sake of the pleasure of all beings;
therefore, they are remembered as mothers.
Having given those cows of Surabhi’s lineage,
one is glorified in the heavenly world;
therefore, I shall describe them.
And their gift, according to the rule— by whatever rite it is to be given, and to whomsoever it is to be given.
Indeed, for the sake of nourishing a twice-born man, or for the purpose of a sacrificial cow,
the first [gift] is a tawny cow.
The second was yellowish-brown;
the third was reddish-tawny;
the fourth was dark-blue and tawny.
The fifth is Śuklapiṅgākṣī; the sixth is Śuklapiṅgalā;
and the seventh is Citrapiṅgākṣī.
The eighth is Babhru-rohiṇī; the ninth is Śvetapiṅgākṣī;
the tenth is Śvetapiṅgalā.
Such oxen as those are proclaimed to be Kapilas;
a Brāhmaṇa may indeed cause them to be driven.
There is never another color for one who has given a cow of good disposition, provided with a pillow,
possessing a beautiful calf, and yielding milk.
O King, for as many hairs as there are on the cow,
for that many years one who gives away a tawny cow with her calf shall be granted all his desires.
With a bronze milking vessel and golden tips on her horns,
that cow— having become a wish-fulfilling cow through those various qualities— approaches the man who gives her away.
He who gives a thousand cows adorned with all desirable things,
having attained supreme prosperity and glory, [attains the highest state].
He is glorified in the heavenly world; moreover, after death, he shall go for ten births to the worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Having given cows according to the prescribed rule,
or he who, having purchased cows with wealth obtained through inheritance, bestows them;
And for him who, having won wealth through gambling, [gives it away], there are inexhaustible worlds both here and in the hereafter.
He who, having purchased cows, bestows them,
shall go to the stainless worlds;
and he who, having accepted them, gives them away [likewise].
Having gone to that difficult-to-reach place with a pure mind,
he rejoices together with the immortals.
And he who, having sold himself, should give cows according to the prescribed rule,
goes to the stainless worlds.
He who, having abandoned his body in battle, gives away cows after purchasing them, dwells in happiness like a god.
They are the price for the sale of one's body;
they are eternal, milking forth all desires, endowed with beauty, and possessed of virtuous character and youth.
For all cows that possess fragrance are indeed praiseworthy;
just as the Gaṅgā is the most excellent among rivers,
so too is the Kapilā the most excellent among Arjunī cows.
Those born within [the household], those obtained through fair purchase or sacrificial rites,
those who have given up their lives, those brought with water and firewood, and those surrendered after being rescued from hardship— all these have come for the sake of nourishment.
Through these gateways, these specific cows are most excellent.
Having fasted here for three nights, the donor should give cows that have been satisfied to those who have been gratified.
Having given cows whose udders have been sucked by their calves and which are provided with bedding for three days, one should subsist on cow-products;
such a person is the eldest in the world, conducting themselves according to the ways of the world.
Praised by the Vedas, being the very essence of the flow of Soma,
gentle, meritorious, and bestowers of desires as well as life— by giving cows, the virtuous always remain virtuous.
Nor is mere giving alone praised for these cows;
rather, the recipient, the time, the specific nature of the cow, and the ritual procedure must be considered.
Having seen that cows are like fire and the sun, one should act accordingly.

To one who is rich in Vedic study, a preeminent recipient, distinguished, established in the sacrificial fires, truthful in speech, grateful, patient toward cows, a refuge for cows, and of virtuous conduct— Vdha_059.017–059.018.
A vessel is praised for the gift of a cow, as is land and gold at all times; furthermore,
the gift of alms is highly commended.
The gift of water and likewise the gift of food;
to one who begs and has many dependents, a cow should be given with diligent effort.
For even that single [gift] yields an exceedingly great fruit,
O King, if one sells it with words defiled by impurity.
Such a man is not praised as a Brahmin;
he is not even considered a Brāhmaṇa.
A cow must never be given to him under any circumstances.
If one gives that which is worn out and already used,
like a fruitless old well,
the giver enters into darkness.
Those who cause a twice-born man to suffer through affliction,
those who are wicked, emaciated, or even rulers—
such as these are not worthy of receiving gifts.
He who yokes a learned Brahmin with fruitless labors shall go to the animal realm and to worlds devoid of fruit;
yet he who gives a well-behaved ox as a gift [attains the opposite].
One who gives ten cows attains the worlds of Yugaṃdhara, the bearer of the plough, who possesses infinite heroism, strength, and youth.
That man who bestows upon a twice-born a dark-blue bull, endowed with strength,
possessing six limbs, pleasing, and handsome;
To the eminent Brāhmaṇa, he gave a lordly bull— youthful, powerful, dark-hued, and the leader of a herd of a hundred.
Those who bestow a bull adorned with many horns go to that world of cows.
Greater than the worlds of the gods, having remained there for a very long time,
they are thoroughly satiated with all their desires.
They are born into positions of sovereignty,
being born again and again with cows that have horns of gold and silver and are accompanied by sacrificial gifts.
A cow made of bell-metal with a milk-pail of the same, adorned with a golden cloth,
and accompanied by sesame seeds and a golden cloth— by such a gift,
the worlds of the Vasus become unshakable for him.
But he who, restrained by his vows, should give a cow made of ghee when sesame seeds are unavailable,
is delivered from misfortune by that cow.
He is honored in the world of Brahmā. Furthermore, he who, restrained by his vows, gives a water-cow when ghee cannot be obtained, [attains the same reward].
He crosses over every difficulty and enjoys divine water; indeed,
he honors both Brahmins and cows.
One family has been divided into two parts:
on one side the mantras abide,
and on the other side the sacrificial oblation abides.
But he who, having approached, should give cows with a pure mind— for as many hairs as there are on them—
For that long he is glorified in heaven;
now hear from me about the worlds of cows— what they are like and where they are situated.
They are pleasing and delightful,
always yielding all desires; they are meritorious and indeed destroyers of sin.
There is no doubt that they reach the worlds of cows;
there, in that great place, they rejoice as those who possess ultimate happiness.
Those men, free from all taint,
travel in celestial chariots like planets that have ascended into the sky.
Thus, those by whom honors were bestowed,
who are ever fragrant and worshipped, who can assume any form at will, are the great-souled ones.
Purified and freed from sin, they possess power equal to that of the gods and rejoice with hosts of apsarases.
They are sung of by the Gandharvas;
there is no doubt that they are a refuge for cows,
devoted to Brahman, and of virtuous conduct.
Compassionate, sympathetic, merciful, and performers of auspicious deeds, they rejoice together with the immortals.
Just as a fish in the water is carried along with the water, so too is the evil deed of a wrongdoer carried away by the cows.
I am indeed firmly carried away;
mothers are remembered as the protectors of all beings and of their offspring.
O King of kings, cows are the essence of the world according to Brahmā; they remove both sin and fear. When they are given as gifts, [all these benefits are attained].
What could possibly not be given here, especially to one who is emaciated, distressed for want of livelihood, and perishing?
"There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to the gift of land," so say those who know the Dharma.
Listen as I declare this to you:
the giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years.
The one who seizes [the gift] and the one who consents to it shall dwell in hell for exactly that long;
however, for all [others], an excessive gift [is likewise a fault].
The gift of land is described here:
for land is immovable and inexhaustible;
it bestows all desires.
The giver of land, having ascended to heaven,
thrives for eternal years; and having attained birth once again, he prospers.
He shall certainly become a lord of the earth,
just as the Goddess Earth always makes the donor her husband.
In this way, when a cow is given along with a sacrificial fee,
she redeems even a king who has committed evil deeds.
Accept the giver of land;
one who gives land shall become purified,
for the earth is indeed meritorious.
Her name is indeed Priyadattā; this is her eternal secret, which constantly brings her joy.
Whatever sin a man oppressed by his livelihood may commit, it is bestowed [as a gift] by one who recites this praise.
One is purified even by the gift of land the size of a cow’s hide,
as well as by the gift of gold, silver, and copper.
O one of great wisdom, he who gives the earth gives all these things: jewels, pearls, and riches.
Austerity, sacrifice, sacred learning, virtuous conduct, freedom from greed, truthfulness,
and the worship of gurus and deities.
Devoted to the supreme welfare of their master, they do not overstep the giver of the earth;
having surrendered their lives, they are slain in battle.
Having gone to the world of Brahmā, those who have given land tilled by the plow do not fall away from that state.
Whether accompanied by water and fruit,
or even merely a shelter with water,
one attains my prosperity.
He who gives to a twice-born man the earth strewn with jewels is liberated from all impurities.
Those who bestow upon Brahmins land covered with sugarcane are glorified in the heavenly world.
Those who give a cow that milks all desires to a preeminent brahmin do not approach Yama.
A man who makes a gift of land goes to the world of Brahmā;
he is liberated from great fear.
Indeed, no other gift excels the gift of land;
for land is meritorious and possesses all flavors.
O bull among men,
the worlds of that high-souled giver of land do not perish.
Just as a mother nourishes her own son with milk, O King,
so does the earth possess all virtues.
One prospers after the giver by performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees.
O King, one does not obtain that fruit which is gained by giving the earth,
for the servants of Death indeed wield their rods of punishment.
The most terrible torments of fire and the horrific nooses of Varuṇa do not approach the giver of land.
The ancestors dwelling in the world of the fathers and the gods dwelling in the celestial realm gratify the donor.
To one who is the best among those possessing land, who is emaciated, whose servants are emaciated, whose livelihood is exhausted, and who is perishing;
By giving land that provides a means of livelihood, a person becomes a performer of sacrificial sessions (*sattra*); likewise, by giving a lion-throne and an umbrella, he attains the same merit.
