salutations to the one clad in yellow garments, the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Salutations to the one who is for all, to the one with the beautiful crown, to the Imperishable;
salutations to the one dear to devotion, to the boon-granting one with the radiant Sudarśana; salutations to the Lord of All, to the boon-granter, to the Excellent One.
Salutations to the soul of the universe, the cause of the supreme cause, the Lord of Yoga, the Victorious One, the most excellent,
the refuge of the worlds, and the refuge of the thirty gods.
I am forever bowed in homage to Mahāvarāha,
to Nārāyaṇa, the primordial deity and the cause, who is inconceivable, unmanifest, and of infinite forms.
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, the ancient Puruṣa remaining at the end of the aeon, the Lord of Yoga, who wears a beautiful and variegated crown.
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is to be known, the foremost, standing beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), self-born, and most excellent.
The great seers who know Brahman speak of him as the eternal Puruṣa, the Lord of the gods, who is invisible, indivisible, and without beginning or middle.
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva,
whom they call the imperishable, all-pervading Brahman;
by perceiving whom one is liberated from the jaws of death.
I approach that Lord Viṣṇu, the eternal refuge, who is satisfied by incomparable qualities,
the effect, the action, and the cause, and who is immeasurable.
I go for refuge to Viṣṇu, Janārdana, who has a golden navel and the excellent lotus-navel, who possesses great strength, who is a treasure-house of the Vedas, and who is the supreme among gods.
I take refuge in Keśava, who wears yellow garments, who is variegated with golden ornaments, who bears a garland,
who is the source of existence, and the most excellent among those who know the Vedas.
I take refuge in the Lord, the imperishable one who has become the Self, the soul of yoga, the most eminent among the knowers of Sāṃkhya,
the great god marked with the Śrīvatsa.
I take refuge in the unsurpassed secret of the Vedas, which is subtle, immovable,
and bestows fearlessness upon its devotees.
I take refuge in the Supreme Lord, the source of all worlds, who is devoid of qualities and who is sought by those free from attachment.
The supreme goal of ascetics,
the Blessed One, the presiding lord of the gods,
the imperishable one with lotus-like eyes.
With devotion, I take refuge in the one worthy of refuge, the beloved of the Brahmins, Trivikrama, the Lord of the three worlds.
I take refuge in Madhusūdana, the primordial, the one, the stainless, the self of all beings, and the Great Soul.
The primordial god, the unborn Śambhu, Janārdana who is both manifest and unmanifest,
the Knower of the Field, the Puruṣa, the Sacrifice.
I take refuge in Nārāyaṇa, the supreme lord, who transcends the three qualities, is imperishable, and is subtler than the subtlest.
Salutation to the one who is beyond the three worlds, the Supreme Self, the one with a thousand heads.
To the infinite, great-souled one— the excellent, faultless God—
the sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas [offer salutations].
I take refuge in that eternal one whom all proclaim;
salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one.
O bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees,
O Subrahmaṇya, homage be unto you;
protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
Reflecting upon his devotion,
O King, he became pleased and manifested his presence.
In that lake, Mādhava seized that elephant which had been seized by a crocodile from its dwelling in the water.
Mādhava split the crocodile standing on dry land with his discus and liberated the elephant.
He who had sought refuge from the nooses was indeed Hūhū, the best of the Gandharvas, due to the curse of Devala.
He attained the state of an elephant from Kṛṣṇa,
and having obtained liberation, he went to heaven;
he was instantly released from the curse.
The elephant became a Gandharva; even the crocodile who was struck down by Kṛṣṇa attained the state of a Yakṣa.
His release from that curse was brought about by Jaigīṣavya;
Govinda, being well-pleased, protects him.
Even when enraged, he instantly delivers his enemies from the ocean of worldly existence and bestows upon them divinity.
And having regained their respective forms, the king of the Gandharvas and the Yakṣa both prostrated before Janārdana.
"O mighty-armed one, the God of gods spoke these words as he attained supreme liberation."
Having seen that the elephant and the crocodile were liberated,
the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana [beheld] both the crocodile and the king of serpents.
And he, possessing a firm resolve, shall remember me,
this lake, and likewise the liberation of you two.
The thicket of hollow bamboos,
that excellent mountain,
as well as the Aśvattha tree, Bhāskara, and the Gaṅgā.
And those mortals who shall remember the Naimiṣa forest, or who shall listen to this properly, [shall attain the highest state].
Due to my protection, they shall not suffer the consequences of the evil of bad dreams; they shall be liberated from all sins.
And those men shall become partakers of auspicious things, and likewise they shall go to a meritorious destination.
For those men, bad dreams shall become good dreams;
[they shall hear] the Kūrma, the Mātsya, and the Vārāha [Purāṇas].
As well as Vāmana and Tārkṣya, and likewise the form of Nārasiṃha—
having risen in the morning, [one should contemplate] these.
Those men who shall remember this,
O king of kings, go to the supreme goal; having spoken thus, [he departed].
Then Janārdana, the god of gods,
touched the Gandharva Gaja and caused him to seize that Yakṣa.
Touched by him, both immediately reached their desired celestial chariot and went to the abode of the gods.
Then Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the gods,
having liberated that excellent elephant,
was indeed praised by the sages.
Through secret Vedic words and syllables,
that Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the Sovereign whose course is difficult to comprehend, has departed.
Having witnessed the liberation of the lordly elephant, all [the gods], led by Indra and placing Brahmā at their head, [approached].
They all stood with palms joined in reverence and paid homage to the high-souled Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
The person who, having risen early in the morning, should constantly hear this,
shall attain supreme perfection.
His bad dreams perish;
one should recite the meritorious *Gajendramokṣaṇa* upon rising in the morning.
One is liberated from all sins,
O best of the Kurus, by faith through remembering, reciting, and narrating [this].
One shall attain a long life. I have narrated to you this divine, purifying, and sin-destroying [account].
Proclaim it, O mighty-armed one;
and listen with devotion, as it is being proclaimed to the brahmins, exactly as it has been told.
Having heard the account of the liberation of the lordly elephant from Bhīṣma, the son of Bhagīrathī, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, [was filled with wonder].
He worshipped Keśava,
as did those best of the twice-born who were standing near the son of Pāṇḍu.
They also bowed down to Vāsudeva, who stood at the side of Bhīṣma—
the most excellent, the most venerable one, whose navel is a choice lotus.
They paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, the treasure-house of Brahman, the Lord of the gods, that secret of the deities, the ancient Puruṣa, the most eminent among those who know Brahman.
O Great King, this merit [is for] men of evil deeds when a terrible bad dream is seen.
Having heard this, one who is devoted to the Lotus-Eyed Lord is liberated from sin;
the elephant was released from suffering.
In the same way, O Indra among kings, you too,
having sought refuge in Hari,
shall be liberated from all sins.
O high-minded one, O one of great wisdom, you shall attain the supreme goal,
even though your bonds of karma are not yet exhausted.
O best of the twice-born, whatever prayer a man should recite at the time of death,
and whatever state of being he should keep in mind—
He attains the supreme state;
tell me that, O great sage—
the one marked with the Śrīvatsa, the seed of the universe.
In the past, Nārada questioned the infinite Lord Nārāyaṇa regarding the cultivation of the world.
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future,
how are you to be meditated upon by devotees who are full of faith and have conquered their senses?
When death is imminent,
what mantra should a man constantly recite,
having risen at dawn?
"O Eternal One, tell me that which occurs while one sleeps, wakes, and meditates. Having heard this from that divine sage, [the Lord spoke].
The Blessed Viṣṇu, the refuge of the world and skilled in speech, spoke these words to Nārada.
"Behold, O sage, I shall tell you of the divine *anusmṛti*,
by recollecting which at the time of death— "
Having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, and having recollected me with a mind fixed on me, he attains the supreme goal.
Becoming single-minded and disciplined,
one should utter this mantra:
"The unmanifest, eternal God."
With palms joined in reverence, I take refuge in Viṣṇu, the infinite Supreme Person,
the infallible Supreme Lord.
I take refuge in Viṣṇu, the ancient and supreme, the wonderful creator of the worlds,
the lotus-eyed one.
I have taken refuge in the Lord who is compassionate toward his devotees, the protector of the world,
the imperishable, supreme state.
I have taken refuge in the Blessed One,
the creator of all beings, the lotus-navelled Hṛṣīkeśa.
I have attained the true and imperishable Hiraṇyagarbha, who contains the earth within himself,
the immortal one whose face is turned in every direction.
I take refuge in the radiant one, without beginning or end, possessing the splendor of the sun,
the god with a thousand heads.
I take refuge in Vaikuṇṭha, whose vehicle is Tārkṣya— the subtle, immovable, most excellent, and bestower of fearlessness.
Nārāyaṇa, Nara, Haṃsa,
the eternal soul of yoga,
the refuge of all the worlds.
I take refuge in the eternal Lord,
who is the master of all worlds and by whom all this is pervaded.
May that Lord Viṣṇu, the teacher of all things moving and unmoving, be gracious to us— he from whom Brahmā was born in ancient times.
May Padmayoni, the Grandfather, be gracious to us; may Viṣṇu— our father, mother, and grandfather— be gracious to us.
He who, when the dissolution has arrived and the world of moving and non-moving beings has perished,
remains alone as the self of yoga.
May that Viṣṇu be gracious to us— He who [is praised] with four and four,
and with two and five.
And he is invoked again by two [mantras]:
"May that Viṣṇu of ours be gracious; may Parjanya, the earth, and the crops [prosper]."
May Vāsudeva— the time, the dharma, the action, the fruit, and the mine of all virtues— be gracious to us, O tawny-hued one.
Obeisance to you, O abode of yoga;
O abode of all, granter of boons; O womb of sacrifice, O highly fortunate one!
Obeisance to you, the fivefold sacrifice;
O four-formed one, the abode of the universe; O dwelling place of Lakṣmī, the bestower of boons.
Homage to you, O Abode of All! Homage to you, O Lord of the World, who have become the witness! O Invincible One, O Wielder of the Broken Axe!
O Viśvamūrti, O Vṛṣākapi, O Trigarta, O knower of the five times,
salutations to you, O ocean of knowledge.
From the unmanifest the cosmic egg was produced;
that Lord who is prior to the unmanifest is supreme,
for there is nothing higher than him.
I have gone to him for refuge—
he who is the Lord constantly meditated upon by Brahmā, Īśāna, and the others.
They do not attain certainty;
I have gone for refuge to that Great-Souled One who has conquered his senses.
Having reached which they do not return—
to that I have gone for refuge;
by a single part [of him], the entire world [is pervaded].
I have gone for refuge to that all-pervading Teacher who stands firm, having mastered [all things], who is ungraspable and devoid of qualities.
For that gentle light situated in the midst of the sun is what they call the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
May that Great-Souled One be gracious— He who is unmanifest, without fixed abode, difficult to know, and eternal.
Established in primordial nature,
that Great-Souled One experiences it; may that Knower of the Field, who experiences through five modes, be gracious.
May that Great-Souled One, who experiences primordial nature through its many qualities as well as the qualities of the mind,
be gracious.
The Sāṃkhyas, the Yogins,
and others who are perfected great seers—
having known him, they are liberated.
May that Great-Souled One be gracious. Homage to you, O Auspicious One in every way; homage be to you, O Unchanging One.
O witness residing within the heart,
O one beyond the senses, salutations to you;
you are inferred from your signs.
But those who do not recognize you wander through the cycle of existence,
[failing to know] the bodiless one residing within the body.
It is equal in all embodied beings—
the unmanifest, intellect, ego, the great elements, and the senses.
Those [qualities] are not in you, nor are you in them; you are neither they nor are they yours.
You are the creator, the enjoyer, and the immutable one.
He is the Lord and Master of all qualities;
he is the non-agent, devoid of causes, the Sovereign established in his own self.
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one;
salutations be to you once again.
You are the Lord, O Protector of the World.
What more than this can be said?
O God, O Lord of the Thirty-three, meditate upon that which is for the welfare of your devotees.
May I have no further connection with living beings in this birth,
whether through egoism or through the intellect.
Likewise, through qualities such as goodness (*sattva*) and the rest,
may neither dharma nor adharma accrue to me in my future birth.
May I never again have contact with sense objects or even the senses; let my sense of smell go to the earth.
Let my tongue go to the water;
let my eye go to the fire; let my sense of touch go to the wind.
Let sound enter into space; likewise, let the mind enter into the transformative principle (vaikārika),
and let my ego-sense enter into the intellect.
May my intellect be united with You,
and may there be for me a separation from all the senses, the qualities, and the elements.
May sattva, rajas, and tamas enter my primordial nature (prakṛti),
and may [I attain] the state of absolute oneness.
I go unto you, the Supreme; let there be union with you alone;
may there be no further birth for me.
Homage to that Blessed One,
to Viṣṇu, the all-powerful;
with my mind fixed on you and my life-breath gone to you.
O God, being your devotee and having you as my supreme refuge,
I shall remember only you when death has arrived.
May those diseases committed by me in previous bodies enter into me, and may sufferings afflict me.
I discharge whatever debt I owe; let the diseases that have been accumulated by me in the past take possession of me.
Free from debt, I desire to go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu,
belonging to that Blessed One.
And he is my Lord of the Gods; I am never lost to him,
nor is he ever lost to me.
Homage to that Blessed One by whom all this is pervaded;
to him alone have I taken refuge.
Whoever has me, and I who belong to him—
let them constantly recollect this Vaiṣṇava remembrance which destroys all sins.
Whoever recites this while sleeping or waking,
or whoever remembers it at the three junctions of the day— even when death has arrived— [shall attain the supreme goal].
But whoever should keep this in mind,
even if they are of sinful conduct, they too go to the supreme goal.
Whether he worships the God at home, offers a bali-oblation, performs fire-sacrifice, or even merely remembers Him;
He attains the supreme goal,
especially on the full moon day, the new moon day, and on the twelfth lunar day.
One should cause those who have faith, as well as others who have taken refuge in me, to hear this;
and whoever should simply say "Namaḥ" (Salutation).
O Nārada, for my devotee who is endowed with faith— even if he be an outcaste dog-cooker— his worlds shall be imperishable.
How much more so those virtuous ones who sacrifice to me according to the prescribed rites, and meditate upon me in accordance with the rule?
They go to the supreme goal;
he who would perform [this] a thousand times does not attain that state.

Whatever is obtained by my devotees— the sacrifices performed, the gifts given, the austerities practiced, the Vedas studied, and whatever vows and observances were kept— [all that is attained through devotion].
All this ends in destruction,
but for knowledge there is no end;
therefore, one should give to the virtuous.
The practice of giving and other virtues, though righteous and providing fearlessness to beings, is finite in this world;
however, my devotee does not meet with an end.
One who would bestow the knowledge of the Blessed One,
or perform the teaching of the Dharma,
or give away the entire earth— [these are equal].
But it is not equal in any way during hardships, calamities, or alarms, nor when one is besieged by bandits.
One should glorify me by my names:
may Varāha protect me in the water,
and Vāmana in difficult terrains.
May Rāma, Rāma,
and Rāma protect [us] from the evil of bandits; and may Narasiṃha protect us in the forest.
May Keśava protect me from all sides; he has girded his loins for the sake of proceeding toward liberation.
For those men whose sins have been exhausted, the two syllables "Ha-ri" are uttered by them but once.
Devotion to Kṛṣṇa arises for those who,
having gone again and again, return;
[so too do] the planets, such as the moon and the sun.
Even now they do not turn back;
there is no blessing higher than Vāsudeva,
and nothing more purifying than Vāsudeva.
There is no deity higher than Vāsudeva;
by bowing down to Vāsudeva, one does not suffer.
Therefore, O divine sage, [seek refuge] in me alone.
Meditate always without weariness;
from that you shall attain perfection and you will surely behold the eternal state.
Thus enlightened by the God of gods, Nārada cultivated devotion toward Keśava.
Therefore, O Lord of the Earth, you should perform this;
whoever recites it with supreme devotion shall attain equality with Viṣṇu.
This [account] is meritorious, a destroyer of sins,
auspicious, and a dispeller of evil dreams;
by it, sin is utterly destroyed.
Tell me that by which merit increases, by reciting which one goes to a happy rebirth, and by hearing which that occurs.
There was once a certain base Kṣatriya, a hater of Brahmins, a slanderer,
wicked, and one who delighted in tormenting others.
By his very nature he was merciless; he always treated others with contempt, and he was likewise intent upon the wives of others.
His mind became deeply devoted [to that practice]. When his lifespan was exhausted,
he was born as a terrible night-stalker (niśācara).
Indeed, due to that fault of his own karma, he, the foremost among evildoers,
thereafter made his livelihood through cruel deeds alone.
Especially in his state as a Rākṣasa,
that sinner performed [deeds] through his actions;
thus it was for him who was devoted to sin.
Indeed, hundreds of years passed for him due to that very fault of his actions,
and no other means of livelihood appealed to him.
O tiger among men, whatever being the Rākṣasa saw, he seized and devoured it.
Thus, as that exceedingly wicked man came within the range of his arms while committing the slaughter of living beings, Vdha_069.007–008.
A very long time passed,
and his youth likewise reached its maturity; then he beheld him performing austerities.
To that ascetic who had undertaken his vows,
whose arms were raised, who was highly blessed,
and who was protected on all sides.
Seeing him, that evil-minded and lowest of Rākṣasas rushed with speed toward the Brāhmaṇa.
Desiring to devour him,
he [approached], but the protection that had been established by the Brahmin in all directions remained.
"O Blessed One, that Rākṣasa was repelled by her; what kind of protection did that best of the twice-born provide?"
By which [power] that night-stalker was stripped of his vigor and cast out,
while he remained one-pointed in mind upon Govinda.
Reciting that [mantra] and devoted to it as his supreme goal,
that brahmin performed austerities,
having entered the cage of Viṣṇu.
O best among the upholders of dharma, I desire to hear the Viṣṇupañjara for protection from all fears at all times.
That supreme protection which formerly existed for the one who destroyed Tripura was previously [bestowed] by Brahmā as the Viṣṇu-armor.
O best of the Kurus, he was appointed by Vāgīśa for the protection of Śaṅkara and of Śakra.
I shall describe the form of him who is setting out to destroy Bala; listen to that, O lord of the earth.
Viṣṇu stands in the east bearing the discus;
Viṣṇu is in the south bearing the mace;
Viṣṇu is in the west bearing the Śārṅga bow.
Viṣṇu, bearing a sword, is to my north;
Hṛṣīkeśa is in the intermediate corners,
and Janārdana is in the gaps between them.
Hari in the form of a boar is upon the earth;
Narasiṃha is in the sky before me; and [I hold] the stainless discus with razor-sharp edges.
This Sudarśana wheel revolves; its garland of rays is difficult to behold;
may it slay the night-stalking spirits of the dead.
And this mace, with its thousand rays,
is the destroyer of the Ḍākinīs;
likewise is the twanging of the Śārṅga bow.
May Vāsudeva utterly destroy my enemies— the pretas and others—
who have been shaken off and struck down.
May those Kūṣmāṇḍas and Yakṣas immediately attain gentleness, like serpents before Garuḍa.
Those who are Daityas, those who are night-stalkers, ghosts, Vināyakas, cruel beings,
humans, Jambhakas, and birds—
May those beasts such as lions,
as well as scorpions and serpents,
all become gentle toward you.
Those people who rob me of the fluctuations of my mind, who steal my memory, and who take away my strength and vigor—
Those who cause the loss of one's shadow, those who steal one's enjoyments,
and those who destroy one's auspicious marks;
May those Kūṣmāṇḍas perish; may there be health of the intellect, health of the mind,
and likewise health of the senses.
By the glorification of Vāsudeva, the God of gods, may [this protection] be for me—
behind, in front, to my right, and to my left.
And let Janārdana Hari be situated in the intermediate corner;
by bowing down to that Janārdana— the adorable Īśāna, the infinite Lord— one does not perish.
Just as Hari is the supreme Brahman,
so too is Keśava the very nature of the universe; by the truthful chanting of the name of that Acyuta, [all sins are destroyed].
"May my threefold impurity go to destruction"—
with these words, he established the Viṣṇupañjara for the sake of self-protection.
O King, because of this protection, that Rākṣasa became invincible to wicked beings and Rākṣasas.
At the conclusion of his recitation, that Brahmin saw him cast down upon the ground, shaken off and deprived of his luster.
And having seen him, overcome with compassion,
he comforted the night-stalker and asked the reason for his arrival.
And he related that exactly as it happened;
having told all of that,
the Rākṣasa spoke again:
Be gracious, O best of brahmins;
grant me instruction,
for many sins have been committed by me.
Many have been killed by me, and many women have been made widows with their sons slain.
And the destruction of many sinless beings has been wrought;
O brahmin-sage, I desire [to know] that.
O observer of noble vows, through your grace,
please grant me an instruction in dharma in order to bring about the destruction of this sin.
O night-stalker, how is it that you, who are of such a cruel nature, have suddenly arrived here?
O seeker on the path of dharma,
I had come to devour you,
but I have been repelled by the protection provided by you.
And from that touch, O Brahmin, this wholesome thought has remained in my mind:
"Who is that protector? I do not know her."
I do not know her ultimate destination;
however, having encountered her company,
I have attained supreme world-weariness.
O knower of dharma, show mercy; extend compassion toward me so that my sins may be removed.
"Noble one, do so," [said the demon]. Thus addressed by that compassionate *rākṣasa*, the sage—
The illustrious one replied after reflecting for a very long time:
"That which you have spoken for the sake of instruction," Vdha_070.012.
"Disgusted with my own actions, I say:
this is appropriate; it is not conducive to the cessation of sins."
"I shall [deal with] the Yātudhānas,
but I will not deliver a teaching on the Dharma; therefore,
O gentle one, ask those twice-born ones."
"Those who are indeed devoted to the sacred teachings"—
having spoken thus, the brahmin departed,
and the Rākṣasa fell into deep reflection.
"How might my evil be dispelled?"—
with his senses thus agitated, he no longer devours living beings at that time.
Though tormented by hunger,
he would eat only a single creature at every sixth mealtime.
Once, overcome by hunger, as he was wandering through the forest, he then saw one who was eating fruit.
He saw the brahmin Kauśika before him;
hungry, he seized him for the sake of food at his sixth mealtime.
A student who had come for the sake of his guru and was subsisting on fruits was seized by that Rākṣasa.
Then that young sage,
despairing of his life, spoke with conciliatory words to the night-stalker.
"O gentle-faced one, tell me truly what business it is for which I have been seized by you here."
"Here I am; instruct me. You have come at the sixth mealtime to me who am hungry."
O night-stalker, if you must certainly devour me, you who are merciless and hostile toward the twice-born; Vdha_070.021–021.
"I shall return this very day after reporting the fruit [of my merit] to my guru; having come to the presence of my guru, I shall do so."
That which was done by me as the taking of fruit— now that I have reached my end here— that has been reported for the sake of my sin.
Therefore, wait for me right here for just a moment,
until I have informed my guru.
"I come here for the sake of fruit;
O Brahmin, at this sixth mealtime, no one has come to take anything from me."
"Understand this: one is liberated from such a sinful livelihood;
herein, there is only one [path] to liberation."
Listen to that reason of mine; I shall release you without doubt,
provided that you do it.
"O Rākṣasa, I shall do that which does not cause opposition to my guru, nor that which obstructs dharma."
O Brahmin, it is not that I have failed to observe my vows; rather, it is due to my very nature and especially because of the defects of my birth.
"Out of a lack of discernment, sinful deeds were constantly committed by me; from my childhood, I have been devoted to evil acts."
My mind is not inclined toward meritorious deeds;
tell me that by which I may attain liberation from the accumulation of those sins.
Whatever evil deeds I have committed out of ignorance,
having entered this wicked womb.
O twice-born one, tell me of its liberation; O son of a brahmin, if you will explain this to me in its entirety.
Afflicted as you are by hunger, you will certainly attain liberation;
yet I am not one of evil character.
Today, hungry and thirsty at the sixth mealtime, I, cruel-souled and pitiless, shall devour you.
Thus addressed by that terrible Rākṣasa, the son of the Sage fell into deep reflection.
Unable to utter it, the Brahmin, after reflecting for a very long time,
sought refuge in Jātavedas.
Having fallen into a state of supreme doubt, he went to [the sage] for the sake of receiving knowledge, wondering whether the fire had been properly served.
May the seven-flamed fire protect me from that [sin], whether it arises from failing to serve my guru or from not having properly observed my vows.
Neither mother nor father do I regard with such reverence as I do my guru, as I understand it.

The practice of yoga, moderation in speech, avoidance [of worldly distractions], and the observation of clay drums and other [instruments].
Non-attachment, silence of the mind, austerity, contentment with the truths, steadfastness, and the abandonment of greed.
Likewise, O King, this is the possession [of the Self]:
the unwavering conviction that all these beings are Viṣṇu.
Devotion that is unswerving—
these qualities have been declared by me,
as well as these causes of laxity.
When his mind had attained peace through these means, the bondage of karma was severed; Hari, drawn forth by his meditation, remained present before him.
He indeed brings to rest actions that are white,
mixed, or black;
furthermore, listen to the meaning of the scripture.
O Lord of Men, I shall speak in brief how liberation is attained by those seeking release.
But as for the obligatory and occasional rites performed by one free from desire,
as well as those prohibited acts performed by those possessed of desire—
Likewise, O King, there is the non-performance [of forbidden acts],
and unswerving devotion to Govinda, the Lord of all.
It bestows liberation upon men;
let there be no doubt in you regarding this. This has been told in its entirety.
O twice-born one, since you have been asked by me how the pacification of actions comes about for those who desire peace.
However, the pacification of all karmas that you have described here is not their absolute destruction once they have been stilled.
Furthermore, arising will occur again once its own cause is encountered,
just as a small fire [flares up] upon reaching grass.
Therefore, O illustrious one, speak to me with a face gracious with favor,
so that my [karmic] exhaustion may come to pass.
O King, there is no destruction of karmas through the eradication of their roots,
even in ten thousand lifetimes.
Without yoga, there is no destruction of karma;
but the fire of yoga can consume even that which is supreme. O brahmin-sage, [learn] that yoga from me.
O Blessed Hiraṇyagarbha, tell me that by which the exhaustion of all karmas is produced.
Listen to me in brief regarding that yoga which was asked of the ancient sages by Anādi and which he then proclaimed.
Just as knowledge is, O Lord of the Earth,
so too is yoga— which consists of knowledge and is imperishable— the cause for its destruction.
Having heard this through tradition,
the compassionate sages reveal it here for the sake of all living beings.
O King, in ancient times, the gods, the great seers, and all the royal seers went there seeking the highest good.
They said to him, "Kapila is indeed our refuge; you are always compassionate toward all living beings."
Therefore, lift us up who are submerged here in this mire of saṃsāra;
[teach] that which is the highest good for all social classes.
O Lord, tell us that which is more beneficial than even this, for there is nothing else superior to it that brings benefit even to women.
That which is beneficial for human beings— in the beginning, in the middle, and at the end— even for insects and moths;
"Tell us that which is our supreme good.
Thus was Kapila addressed by all the gods as well as the celestial rishis.
"There is nothing superior to yoga," he said long ago;
"just as afflictions [are purified] through tens of thousands of births."
When stability has been attained in the mind, then yoga, accumulated over many births, leads to that peace.
For those men who practice this and have renounced all actions, Viṣṇu quickly attains proximity to them.
For women and Śūdras, there is no means of purification other than Yoga for the sake of peace from their actions and for the sake of liberation.
That nature of yoga which has been practiced by them through many births in auspicious castes and existences— [that very nature arises] for them.
For those men who are established in the state of women or Śūdras,
and for whom there is no practice of yoga acquired in previous births, [the following applies].
For the attainment of yoga,
there is a sequence beginning with Śūdra and Vaiśya;
through womanhood, one attains the state of a Śūdra.
From that he would attain the status of a Vaiśya; thereafter, a Kṣatriya becomes a Brāhmaṇa,
and from that state he becomes devoid of ritual action.
Likewise, one who is learned in the Vedas, a performer of sacrifices, and thereafter devoted to action; then, having attained the state of a knower of reality.
The yogi shall attain liberation through gradual stages; however,
for those whose practice of yoga has been obscured by mere birth, [liberation does not come so easily].
They remain right there; when the cause of birth has been exhausted and the unwholesome karma performed previously has perished, they are liberated.
Since that which bestows birth from non-existence has been consumed by the fire of yoga, whence can there be any power for that birth?
Just as fire with upward-flaming crests, fanned by the wind, burns dry grass,
so does the fire of yoga consume all karmas.
It reduces [the body] to ashes,
just as a seed with its husk burnt; because it is no longer a seed, it does not sprout again.
Likewise, when the afflictions have been burnt away by yoga,
the self is not born again for those who have seen the truth and no longer perceive [the world of phenomena].
Those among yogins who experience a lapse from yoga attain the state of being a yogin once again in this world.
Karma that brings about one's birth was performed by him as that very self; thus do the Brahmins and others proceed to their respective births.
Even there, those who have arisen from many births are carried away by the knowledge of reality,
just as the brahmin Jaigīṣavya was.
Just as Asita and others,
as well as the kṣatriya Hiraṇyanābha, so too were Janaka and the rest.
Through yoga practiced in former lives,
Tulādhāra and others of the vaiśya caste attained supreme perfection.
The Śūdras were Pailavaka and others;
Maitreyī, Sulabhā, Gārgī, and the ascetic Śāṇḍilī.
Even others, such as Dharmavyādha and his like, having attained the female state, achieved supreme perfection through their former practice despite that loathsome condition.
Even those who have attained the status of the lowest caste achieve perfection through hearing [the sacred texts], for that which was practiced by them in former lives remains with them.
The knowledge of yoga belongs to the great-souled ones even without instruction and the like;
therefore, yoga is the supreme good.
For that which bestows the fruit of liberation grants absolute happiness in liberation,
whereas the other happiness is merely delusion.
All this has been told to you by me, O elephant among men—
the highest good that transcends even yoga.
Nothing else remains to be known. O best of sages, you have described the greatness of yoga.
But its true nature has not been told to me;
indeed, O King, I wish to hear about that twofold nature of yoga.
Listen now to that which is both supreme and non-supreme; I shall speak it, for it is the truth to be told to virtuous ones who desire to hear.
Whether one should bestow the knowledge of the Blessed One,
or perform the teaching of the Dharma,
or give away the entire earth—
Nothing else here, O lord of men, is in any way equal to that; other gifts in this world are subject to decay.
The gift of knowledge alone is praised as the single, inexhaustible, and unsurpassed gift;
for all other gifts here in this world yield but a single fruit.
O King, for one who bestows knowledge correctly upon the virtuous throughout the three worlds, what could there be that has not already been given?
O lord of men, other forms of knowledge are insubstantial, like the works of a craftsman;
there is but one supreme knowledge.
That which brings about the attainment of yoga— I am the speaker and you are the listener;
the yoga to be spoken is that which grants liberation.
For the benefit of living beings,
this excellence, augmented by virtues,
[was bestowed] together with the Supreme Brahman.
That oneness with the Self of the King is itself celebrated as yoga;
what other characteristic of yoga could there be?
Furthermore,
O Lord of the Earth, there are two yogas, both of this world and the next; I shall describe their true nature to you.
Therefore, listen here with a one-pointed mind: the Supreme Brahman is pure existence alone, designated as Viṣṇu, and devoid of all distinctions.
Since it is difficult to conceive beforehand, that which is spoken for the sake of attaining it is as follows:
the mind is as flickering as a whirlwind.
O King, because Brahman is subtle, it is without an object of perception and without a locus; it is ungraspable,
for its nature is ungraspable.
For one who practices correctly and incessantly,
even over the course of hundreds of other births, he is born as one from whom Brahman may be received.
O lord of men, if there is no withdrawal due to the fault of obstacles for a yogin established in yoga, [then he attains success].
O King, what could one say of those who bestow perfect knowledge, which is like falling from the very tip of a palm tree?
O King, one who is enriched by higher knowledge attains that supreme Brahman without great hardship.
The Brahman known as Viṣṇu is difficult for a human being to attain; hear now another means for its attainment.
Having fashioned a beautiful image of Viṣṇu that brings him joy,
O King, one should [consider] its characteristics.
Listen as I speak of what materials are required and what her form should be when she is to be fashioned for the rite of meditation.
[One may fashion it] from gold, silver, or copper, or likewise from brass, or even from stone, wood, or clay.
Or one should have it made from a written document; the Lord Viṣṇu should be depicted there with a gentle form and four arms.
The glorious one, adorned with the *śrīvatsa* mark, wearing a crown and garlands,
possesses beautiful eyes and a radiant countenance.
With a beautiful forehead and lovely eyebrows, with fine lips and handsome cheeks, he shone with a radiant countenance.
Adorned by his neck with its auspicious lines, by his ears,
and by the triple-folded furrows of his waist;
Adorned with beautiful ornaments, he has excellent feet and a pair of shapely thighs;
on his left side is the goddess Gadā.
The discus of the god should be placed in his right hand, the conch in his left hand,
and the brilliantly shining lotus in the right.
One should not direct the gaze upward, downward, or sideways;
the Blessed One has his eyes closed.
Janārdana is not to be praised;
rather, a gentle gaze should be maintained,
as if slightly smiling.
The placement of the feet should be performed so that they are well-established on all sides,
with the space between the feet remaining correctly positioned.
The goddess Earth should be fashioned bearing her supreme form,
exactly as it appears in the mind.
The wise man should have such [an image] made; having projected Brahman into it,
he should become absorbed in that through his mind.
One should worship her, one should bow down to her;
one should remember her, one should contemplate her. While worshipping her and bowing down to her, [one attains liberation].
Remembering her and contemplating her, he,
having cast off all defects,
enters that very [energy] which has the form of Brahman.
One should cultivate the contemplation of the king’s own self-form therein; one's mind should not be led elsewhere.
O Lord of the Earth, when the intellect is purified even slightly in some respect by means of restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), the self becomes pure.
One should always worship the form of the Blessed One, being entirely absorbed in Him,
as well as the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas).
O Bhārgava, I wish to hear by what means a yogi, having shaken off all impurity, becomes a partaker of liberation.
Non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing—
these *yamas* have been described to you;
now hear from me the *niyamas* as well.
Austerity, meditation on the Lord,
and observances— O best of the Kauravas, by means of these excellent fundamental virtues, [one attains success].
Likewise, for one who possesses devotion to Viṣṇu and is full of faith, learn from me the other ancillaries of yoga.
O King, the breath that is steady in the middle [channel],
which bestows happiness, auspicious, and pure,
leads to the perfection of yoga.
The posture of the yogins is prescribed; breath control (prāṇāyāma) is the threefold regulation of the vital air;
and retention (dhāraṇā) is the fixing of the vital air in the heart.
O King, know that its divisions are three;
however, there is another, a fourth, which has an objective support (*sālambana*). Vdha 100.006–007.
The external and internal objects are known as the domains of the senses; the intellect, however, [perceives] each of these individually from its own respective object.
The bringing [of the senses] toward the object of knowledge is known by the wise as *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal), for it consists in fixing them upon a single auspicious object.
And that which is the holding of the mind,
because of its immovability, is designated as "dhāraṇā" by the wise.
O King, when that very same concentration (*dhāraṇā*) occurs repeatedly in that very same object, it receives the name "meditation" (*dhyāna*).
Listen also to my teaching on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), O King: having withdrawn the mind from whatever object is to be grasped, one should attend to the mere meaning.
That which appears as the very nature of the object is called *samādhi*;
these have been described to you.
By performing the limbs of yoga individually, excellence arises; by performing them all together, the destruction of that which is to be abandoned occurs.
These limbs of yoga are constituent parts of meditation in their entirety;
and meditation itself, O protector of the earth, [is likewise].
Meditation attains the status of a limb of yoga for those who observe a single vow;
it consists of [discerning] between the wholesome and the unwholesome.
O Lord of Men, he always encounters attachment to worldly objects;
his meditation is turned away from the auspicious.
O King, from that lack of discrimination arises that which clings to the inauspicious and bestows the suffering of saṃsāra.
Having drawn that very [mind] away from wicked sense-objects, a human being reaches the further shore of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
That constant reflection which men have day and night regarding the non-protection of those who grant happiness is meditation (dhyāna) for impure purposes.
"How is this bond of saṃsāra [formed],
and how can there be liberation from it?"— such is the mental disposition of human beings.
This meditation is auspicious and twofold;
it is entirely pure, yet there is still a longing for pleasure even within liberation.
Greed is considered the fruit of what is undesired; meditation is the fruit of both the auspicious and the inauspicious; and that which is neither attached nor averse is desired.
The object of meditation is threefold;
indeed, meditation without an object is not accepted, just as a state of delusion is not.
First, the wise man should practice meditation upon gross objects, and thereafter upon subtle ones. After that, he should meditate [upon the supreme].
O Lord of the Earth, for the sake of pacifying that [affliction] within the atom, one should cultivate only the meditation on its opposite.
The wise man whose mind is absorbed in that becomes identical with it;
therefore,
he should not allow himself to take up any object of focus at an improper time.
O King,
because living beings are driven by the karma produced by their own actions, you have no concern for meditative absorption.
They are beneficial for those who practice meditation,
yet they are all contained within ignorance; for they indeed pertain to the realm of saṃsāra.
And those who have subsequently awakened,
though they are meditators, are not at all benefactors;
for awakening is indeed not innate.
Since even those [qualities] arise from something else,
therefore that Brahman is stainless and possesses consciousness by its very nature.
That supreme state of Viṣṇu, which is the object of meditation for those who know how to meditate— that cannot be attained by sacrifices nor by gifts.
Neither by austerities nor by those vows do they behold the eternal one; with one-pointed minds, they perceive him through meditation alone.
And that is the supreme form of Viṣṇu— indescribable, unborn, and eternal—
from which everything proceeds.
And wherein it attains dissolution—
that which is sleepless, unborn, without dream,
formless, nameless, and eternal.
Yogis who have shaken off both merit and sin behold that eternal one, who is visible through knowledge.
They thus enter the Lord,
that all-pervading Brahman,
Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords.
The Supreme Self is declared to be supreme,
the Lord of lords possessing infinite power,
self-established, and incomparable.
Yogins behold that eternal Blessed One, in whom all is and from whom all proceeds.
Those who are yogis perceive that Blessed One, the eternal, who is everything and from whom everything comes.
Yogis behold Him who is the cause of creation and so forth, whose powers arise from His very own nature.
They enter that eternal Lord, the imperishable Bhagavān, from whom all merit and sin have been shaken off.
There, the yogis who possess yoga clearly behold that eternal Blessed One.
O Lord of Men, you ought to hear from me as I describe that which has been declared regarding the characteristics of a man.
The mind of the yogin, when withdrawn from everything and established in Brahman alone, brings about spiritual perfection.
The stability of the mind, established in Brahman, remains unchanging like a lamp in a windless place.
Such is the characteristic of success for the yogin whose mind is thus one-pointed:
merit and demerit [are exhausted] without remainder.
O King, it goes toward destruction except through the exhaustion of that karma which initiated the body; [this practice] brings about the exhaustion of karma.
O protector of the earth, hear also the definition of that yoga which is declared to be the supreme Brahman.
The dissolution of the mind within that which is called Viṣṇu— the unborn and the imperishable—
is designated as Yoga.
When that mind has dissolved,
the Puruṣa, due to the absence of a cause,
no longer perceives any differentiation.
O lord of men, the distinction between self and other is constructed by knowledge;
when that [knowledge] ceases, there is no longer [distinction] between self and other.
For this very non-separation of the Supreme Self and the individual self,
O scorcher of foes, is indeed the absence of division.
That very supreme yoga has been described to you in brief,
just as when a water-pot is broken.
Just as water that has entered into water attains unity, so too do these two [the individual soul and the Supreme] attain oneness through the destruction of their causes.
Just as fire cast into fire attains equality, becoming identical with it and consisting of that very essence; so too does he.
It is not perceived as distinct;
thus, through the union of Brahman and the self, their state of non-action is established.
No distinction arises between him and [the Absolute], just as there is no difference between the space within a jar and the vast sky; indeed,
he has exhausted all residual karma.
When a person consists of Brahman,
then his true nature cannot be brought within the scope of what has been spoken.

Just as the space within a jar is not distinct from the [universal] sky when the jar is destroyed, so too [the individual soul is not distinct] from Brahman when the objects of abandonment are destroyed.
Likewise, when the skin is pierced by the one named Viṣṇu,
the person is no longer distinct from the wind, just as air [is not distinct] from the wind itself.
But when the bonds of merit and sin are exhausted,
the self, together with Brahman,
then [attains] all auspiciousness.
Then, indeed, he attains another, incomparable, and eternal joy,
for he has become of the very nature of Brahman.
O Indra among kings, he remains eternally concealed within the self at the time of departure.
Just as the stainlessness of a mirror shines forth due to the absence of impurities,
even so does that joy of the self manifest.
Just as moonlight is not created,
so too the abandonment of faults and the knowledge of the self are not created.
The sky does not create water;
it is always manifested [from it].
How can there be the arising of that which is non-existent?
Just as qualities such as awakening are manifested— not produced— through the destruction of the multitude of things to be abandoned; Vdha_100.057.
O lord of men, knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and righteousness are eternally present for the welfare of the self.
For the self that has become Brahman,
these four are eternally non-dual; this is declared to be non-duality.
This yoga has been declared to you;
this is Viṣṇu, this is Brahman,
and likewise this is the supreme truth.
Furthermore, O lord of the earth, listen once more as I describe this in brief: his true nature.
This Self, known as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
when joined with the qualities of primordial nature (prākṛta-guṇa),
becomes pure once those very qualities have departed.
The Supreme Self is declared [to be the object]; Brahman is the object of meditation, the Person is the meditator,
and the means is that which is designated as meditation.
But that which abides within these instruments— O King, what division could there be for that which belongs to their class, even in brief?
Furthermore, hear in brief that which a father should say to his son, or a teacher to his own disciple.
There is nothing higher than Vāsudeva;
there is nothing spoken that is higher than Vāsudeva.
Vāsudeva, the immeasurable Self, is the supreme truth.
Homage, homage to Vāsudeva eternally! Therefore, worship Him; meditate on the Lord;
worship Ananta with an unwearied mind.
By those desiring to reach the further shore of saṃsāra,
Hari alone is to be propitiated;
when propitiated, he grants the objects desired by those who long for wealth.

To those seeking dharma, Viṣṇu grants dharma and all things pertaining to dharma without exception; to those whose minds are set upon desires, he grants those very desires; and to those seeking liberation, Viṣṇu is indeed the bestower of liberation.
O Sage, this which rests upon the knowledge of the Self has been fully told to me;
now I desire to hear something else.
Therefore, being pleased, tell me this:
what is this liberation that has been described by the Blessed One for me according to the sequence of the social classes?
In this regard, O Sage, I wish to hear about the ascent from one caste to a higher caste: how a Śūdra indeed attains the status of a Vaiśya.
O best of the twice-born, how did a Vaiśya become a Kṣatriya, O Bhārgava,
and how did he subsequently attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa?
O great sage, I wish to hear how one attains the fitness for liberation through the state of being a Brahmin.
O delighter of the Bhṛgus,
this subsequent question is appropriate for you;
O best of the Kurus, listen to it.
I shall speak in its entirety that which is beneficial to all social classes, and the duties of the Śūdras without omission.
A Śūdra who acts according to the prescribed rule attains the status of a Vaiśya; and a Vaiśya who performs his own duties attains the status of a Kṣatriya.
O King, a Kṣatriya who is fully devoted to the duties of the twice-born attains the status of a Brahmin,
and a Brahmin attains liberation.
It is appropriate for one who is devoted to honoring all members of every social class who follow their own respective duties.
For those [classes] beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, there is an increase for one who performs inferior deeds and a decrease for one who performs superior deeds.
O King, listen as I describe in due order the duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*), which bestow elevation [from rebirth].
Freedom from envy, compassion, forbearance, purity, auspiciousness, lack of longing,
absence of miserliness, and freedom from exertion.
Likewise, another [type] is common to all castes.
These eight qualities lead to the welfare of men both in this world and in the next.
O tiger among the Kurus,
O King, hear from me the distinct duties of the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas.
But their common means of livelihood is said to be the work of officiating at sacrifices and teaching, O Brahmin.
Likewise, with the acceptance of what is prescribed,
one should provide for dependents and others,
and perform sacrifices when one has the means.
When a twice-born man is no longer capable of maintaining his dependents through his own occupation,
he should then live by resorting to [the following means].
One should completely abandon all those occupations of the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas;
one must not cause a confusion of vocations.
Even in times of distress, it is not commended for a Brahmin to perform the work of a Śūdra,
such as the proper protection of subjects.
O protector of the earth, this is the primary rule ordained for a Kṣatriya:
his livelihood shall be by means of weapons or through service.
With the wealth produced from that,
he may perform all the duties of a Kṣatriya;
and in times of distress, even those of a Vaiśya.
Whatever livelihood is prescribed for the Vaiśya caste— namely, trade,
the tending of cattle, and agriculture— that is indeed ordained.
He should give gifts and perform sacrifices according to the rules with the wealth produced thereby,
as well as with wealth acquired through buying and selling.
A Śūdra may perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices;
he should give desired things to those who seek them, and gifts should be given to him when he serves.
One should likewise provide worn-out clothing, sandals, umbrellas,
and so forth for members of all four castes.
I have declared the Dharma to you;
listen now, O protector of the earth,
to the Dharma of those belonging to the stages of life (āśramas).
Having previously undergone the initiation ceremony,
the religious student (brahmacārī) should perform service to his teacher while residing in the teacher’s house.
Having offered the alms-food to the guru,
one should eat it with his permission after the guru has finished eating.
He should perform service to the sacred fire,
fetch the Vedas, and always bring water for the sake of his guru.
Likewise, he should collect fuel and flowers and other such items;
and while the deity is asleep, he himself should sleep.
He should rise from his bed [only after the teacher has done so], follow him as he walks,
and recite [the text] when called upon by him.
With the mind fixed on that, not looking in any other direction, one who practices the vows correctly with a self-restrained soul should master the Veda.
Jumping like a staff is recommended for bathing, but not for the purification of the limbs;
this applies after having studied one or two Vedas.
Or, having studied the Veda in due order,
he should enter the householder stage of life after giving a sacrificial fee as desired.
Then, O joy of the Kurus, having obtained permission from his guru,
he should dwell in the stage of life of a householder.
A wise man should reach the end by that very means;
therefore, he should resort to the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) or even the fourth stage.
Or he should duly take a wife in the prescribed manner, one who is healthy and born of a noble family.
O King, having acquired wealth, one should marry a suitable wife who is free from physical defects, according to the prescribed rite. Vdha 101.030–101.031.
Endowed with faith, one should perform the daily and occasional rites,
as well as [the honoring of] guests, visitors, and kinsmen.
Likewise, one should satisfy servants and others who are afflicted with food according to one's ability,
as well as birds and even the lowest animals.
O best among the upholders of dharma, approaching one's wife during her fertile season is declared to be the duty even for a householder.
The remnant of the sacrifice is his food;
he should gratify the gods with the *havya* offering and the ancestors with the *kavya* offering according to his ability.
One should always satisfy human beings with food and drink, and one should constantly perform the propitiation of the sages through the private recitation of the Vedas.
One pleases the elements by the offering of bali, Prajāpati by the birth of a son,
and all people by affection.
One should benefit oneself through auspicious action, one's children through instruction,
and one's dependents through providing a livelihood.
A householder should always satisfy [the guests]; food should be given by the master of the home to those who come for alms.
In this way, in the householder’s stage of life, the gods,
the ancestors, and likewise the sages grant all desires.
And when a householder sees that his own body is well-honored by men, yet observes the appearance of wrinkles and grey hair;
Likewise, for the sake of one's offspring,
one should then take refuge in the forest for the sake of the ancestors, the gods, and guests.
In that regard as well, worship is prescribed,
as well as enjoyment in the forest and the emaciation of the self through austerities.
Celibacy, sleeping on the ground, performing fire oblations, bathing at the three periods of the day,
and practicing silence and other such observances are recommended.
In summer, he practiced the penance of the five fires;
during the rainy season, he stayed under the open sky;
and in winter, he slept upon the water.
One should dwell in forest retreats; one should desire massages for the limbs and subsist on fruits and roots as food.
Not entering a village is likewise prescribed as the rule for a forest-dweller;
thus has the dharma of the forest-dweller been declared to you.
Listen as I speak to you, O Bhikṣu, concerning the characteristics of dharma from the beginning, and furthermore, regarding the other stage of life for a mendicant.
One may stay for one night in a village and five nights in a town;
patience and restraint of the senses [are required].
Likewise, O King, non-undertaking, celibacy with meditative concentration,
and the contemplation of the Self.
O King, these duties of a monk have been taught;
this fourth hermitage of a monk has been described by me to you.
This is the rule for men who desire liberation through gradual stages,
according to the duty of their respective castes.
Likewise, by worshipping Hari with the specific duties of one's own stage of life (āśrama), a human being attains perfection.
The student, the householder,
the mendicant, and likewise the forest-dweller— these, performing their own respective duties, [attain success].
For they worship Viṣṇu alone,
O joy of the Kurus, since all the deities, beginning with Brahmā, [are contained within him].
