Thirty *kāṣṭhās* should be known as one *kalā*; thirty such *kalās*, O protector of the earth, constitute one *muhūrta*. Vdha 104.011–104.012.
In that same manner, O best of kings, a month is said to consist of a number of days and nights equal to those [of a day and night].
The southern course consists of six months, and likewise the northern; these two together are known as the two solstices (ayanas).
Time is known as the year;
the southern course (of the sun) is the night of the gods, and the northern course is their day.
One year of the gods is said here to be one day and night,
consisting of three hundred years [of humans].
And sixty times the human count, O Lord of the Earth, constitutes one year even for the gods.
Thus, O King, you should listen correctly as it is being told by me according to the divine measure.
Four thousand years are said to be the Kṛta age; its dawn (saṃdhyā) lasts for as many hundreds [of years].
And the twilight period is of the same duration;
O bull among men, the Tretā age consists of three thousand divine years.
Its morning twilight consists of one hundred years,
and the evening twilight is likewise;
Dvāpara, however, consists of two thousand years.
Of that [Kalpa], it is said that its dawn consists of as many hundreds of years,
and its twilight is likewise of the same duration.
The Kali age lasts for one thousand divine years, O bull among men; its dawn and twilight each last for as many hundreds of years.
And the twilight period was likewise;
first came the Kṛta age,
in which the eternal Dharma prevailed.
Whatever was to be done has already been accomplished at that time as desired by the king;
therein the dharmas do not falter.
And indeed, the subjects do not perish;
therefore, this age is called by the name Kṛtayuga according to its qualities.
In the Kṛta Yuga, O King, there was no non-existence; at that time there was neither buying nor selling, nor were there the divisions of the Sāman, Yajus, and Ṛg Vedas.
There was no human action performed without aiming for a result; no one engaged in dharma without having a motive.
In that conjunction of the ages, there were no diseases, no decay of the senses,
no envy, nor even weeping.
There is no pride nor malice; no conflict, much less sloth; no hatred nor hypocrisy.
There is neither fear nor distress, neither envy nor avarice;
beyond that is the Supreme Brahman.
That which is the supreme goal of yogins,
the Self of all beings,
is then the pure Nārāyaṇa.
In that very Self,
which consists of all worlds, which is imperishable,
and which has assumed whiteness by its own will;
All become stainless:
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas,
and Śūdras who possess the auspicious marks.
In the Kṛta Yuga, the people here are devoted to their own duties,
following their respective stages of life and their respective conduct.
O Indra among kings, the world becomes preeminent in truth and devoted to austerity;
though the dharmas are distinct, they are rooted in a single Veda.
Devoted to this single Dharma, through action joined with the proper time,
they attain the supreme goal.
This Dharma has its characteristics established;
in the Kṛta Yuga, it is eternal for the four castes and possesses all four quarters.
This is called the Kṛta Yuga; now learn from me also about the Tretā,
as to what form it takes when it proceeds.
Dharma diminishes by one quarter,
Viṣṇu turns red,
and men become devoted to falsehood.
From that, sacrifices proceed,
as do various religious duties and rituals; in the Tretā age, they consist of intentional mental dispositions.
From that, the social orders (varṇas) proceeded,
established in their own duties, performing their rites,
and endowed with passion (rajas) due to their state of equality.
In the Dvāpara age as well, dharma proceeds diminished by two parts;
Viṣṇu attains a yellow color.
The Veda itself is fourfold; moreover, there are others who possess four Vedas,
as well as others who possess three Vedas.
Some were knowers of two Vedas, some of one Veda,
and others were devoid of the Ṛgveda;
thus it was when the scriptures had become divided.
When action is directed in many ways toward austerity and charity,
the progeny becomes characterized by passion (rājasī).
Men are short-lived, yet the Veda is very great and difficult to traverse; therefore,
he divides the Vedas into many parts.
Then Hari, in the form of Vyāsa,
[spoke]: "Due to the lack of knowledge regarding *sattva*,
someone remains established in *sattva*."
For those falling away from their virtuous state,
many diseases arose,
as well as desires and calamities.
Then,
being severely oppressed by those things brought about by fate,
human beings perform austerities.
Desiring wealth and desiring heaven,
others perform sacrifices;
thus they act when the Dvāpara age has arrived.
O Indra among kings, through unrighteousness the subjects perish; yet even in the Kali age, O king, dharma remains by one quarter.
Having reached the Tāmasa Yuga, Keśava becomes Kṛṣṇa;
religious observances and proper conduct come to an end.
Likewise, the performance of the sacrifice of Dharma, as well as calamities, diseases, lassitude,
faults such as anger and the like— these are [the obstacles].
Calamities increase, as do mental afflictions, as the ages revolve.
The world revolves again;
when the world has perished, those entities that cause the world to proceed also go to destruction.
They do not even pray for the merits performed during the two previous ages;
O King, this is the Kali Yuga.
O King, in that place where you were born,
he does not manifest an incarnation by means of his own form consisting of a portion of Kṛṣṇa.
In the Kṛta and other ages, Hari protects the world from the Daityas by assuming various forms; but in the Kali age, he enters into another.
The God who assumes a fresh form sustains that which was produced in the past;
Hari is not seen in the Kali age.
Therefore, he is proclaimed as the one who spans the three ages (Triyuga) throughout the Kṛta and other yugas;
and when the end of the Kali age has arrived—
Having entered into Kalki, the expounder of Brahman, Vāsudeva effects the preservation of the world.
In each of those various elements that have arisen previously, the Lord, having entered them, acts during the Kali age.
Whatever Acyuta intends, by his own will, the world becomes white when he is white,
and it is born red when he is red.
When he is yellow, O King, he possesses yellowness; when he is black, he possesses blackness.
He alone is the God of the World.
The creator of the world, the preceptor of the world—
whatever be the form of this God, in that very form the world is born.
The four yugas have been described by you to us in their entirety in brief;
now speak of the Kali age in detail.
O Bhārgava,
I was born when the blessed and stainless Viṣṇu had assumed the state of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of sport.
What will be their food and what will be their conduct at that time— those Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas?
And what will the Śūdras be like, O twice-born one, when the Kali age has arrived?
Tell me that in detail.
In the Kṛta age, austerity is supreme; in the Tretā age, sacrifice alone is indeed the principal thing; in the Dvāpara age, charity is so.
In the Kali age, truth alone [is the means]; in the Kṛta age, there was indeed purification of the mind and austerity without effort.
O King, austerity is accomplished as the supreme means for achieving yoga;
that which is austerity through the mind, O ruler of men, [is the highest].
That austerity is performed for the destruction of the afflictions, not for the sake of liberation;
but in the Tretā age, ritual sacrifices are performed.
Thereafter, O Lord, men perform sacrifices of the mind;
that is the most substantial path of dharma.
In the Dvāpara age, there is not such great learning as there was in the Tretā age;
therefore, the path becomes increasingly coarse.
In the Kali age, men make themselves out to be generous; they possess neither true learning, nor pure wealth, nor purity of mind.
Therefore, truth alone is one;
as is truth, so too are forbearance and non-violence in the Kali age.
Abstaining from harming others is beneficial for men when this terrible age has arrived.
When Kṛṣṇa has attained his dark state,
hear now what the nature of this world becomes here.
O lord of men, kings, brahmins, vaiśyas,
and śūdras alike have become intent upon a dharma of deceit.
People who are like those selling dharma as a commodity diminish the truth in this world by means of men who merely imagine themselves to be wise.
Then, due to their loss of truthfulness, their lifespan will become very short;
and with the exhaustion of their lifespan, their knowledge [will perish].
Those who are devoid of knowledge and lacking in intelligence will not be able to train;
even greed shall overcome them.
Men will become overcome by greed and anger, deluded, subject to desire, and full of enmity.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas,
becoming intermingled with one another,
will become equal to Śūdras.
The lowest will become the middle,
and the middle will become outcasts;
such will the world become.
When Kṛṣṇa has attained blackness,
the finest of garments will be linen,
and among grains, the koradūṣaka.
In the Kali age, men will have wives as their friends;
they will live by means of fish and meat.
O King, at that time, men will become keepers of goats and sheep when their cattle have perished.
On the banks of rivers, they will sow medicinal herbs with spades, yet even those herbs will yield but meager fruit for them.
At the end of the age,
O bull among men, family alliances will cease to be formed outside of one's own lineage.
The faithful will not depart from their homes, nor will they observe religious vows.
Brahmins who revile the Vedas will generally neither perform sacrifices nor offer oblations,
and they will mostly [associate] with the wretched.
Likewise, those endowed with power will forcibly seize the wealth even of those who have family ties and of widows.
Men will harbor desires;
women will harbor desires; no one will ask for a daughter in marriage.
Neither the man who gives the maiden, nor the maiden, nor the suitor shall choose one another by their own will.
At that time, no wife will perform service to her husband;
men, having abandoned the gods and the twice-born, [will act likewise].
The gods, who partake in the sacrificial portions, will turn their faces away from others;
so too will those twice-born ones who have studied the Vedas.
Abandoning those [gods] beginning with Brahmā, men, driven by the power of Time,
become intent on the doctrine of causality (hetuvāda).
At that time, other regions shall likewise subsist on barley as food, and others on wheat as food.
O King, in the Kali age, men will resort to those regions,
yet they will not offer *śrāddha* ceremonies for their ancestors.
Men will offer libations,
they will hold bathing in high regard, and men will not be devoted to ritual purity.
O King, when this age has arrived, the minds of men will no longer be inclined toward devotion to Viṣṇu.
In the first quarter of the Kali age, men will utter insults against Kṛṣṇa, who is characterized by his dark complexion, and against the son of Kṛṣṇa (Kārṣṇi).
"At the end of the age, however, no one at all will take up the name of Hari;
blessed indeed are they, O tiger among men."
In the ocean of sin during the Kali age, those who are themselves sinless shall grasp even the name of Viṣṇu, whose nature is imperishable.
What one attains by meditating on Hari in the Kṛta age, or by performing sacrifices in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, one attains in the Kali age simply by [chanting] His name.
Proclaiming that very name, Hari removes all sins when it is uttered with devotion.
In this world, during the Kali age, people will utter only the name "Vāsudeva."
"Salutation be to Kṛṣṇa here"—
if a virtuous person should speak thus,
[the opponent] will produce delusion by means of the power of his sophistry.
Then, by means of sorcerers among the people,
the heretics will make it exceedingly full of heresy.
O King, this world will then become devoid of respect, and there will be no service rendered to the twice-born.
At that time, the Śūdras will not observe their own duties;
they will falsely assume the outward marks of those who have renounced the world.
There will be those who take bribes, followers of the Sugata, as well as those devoted to the Mahāyāna, and furthermore, heretics.
Likewise, there were Kāpila monks,
as well as elders, Śrāvakas, Nirgranthas, Siddhaputras, and others.
O King, in the Kali age there will be wicked-minded Śūdras who are devoid of purity and possessed of crooked minds.
At that time, there will be wicked-souled Śūdras who have gone forth as renunciants—
these and many others.
O bull among men, there will likewise be heretics, as well as Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
In the Kali age, base men who collect royal taxes will subsist on trade; they will honor neither the twice-born nor the gods.
Men will worship [it] through compositions in the languages of the Mlecchas,
being corrupted by arguments based on mere logic.
Thus, when they have become exceedingly wicked,
others will become wicked as well,
following their path.
O King, at that time men will exist who abide by that moral conduct,
and the world will be filled with such human beings.
At that time, the lifespan of men in this world will be very short,
and even the maximum lifespan will be thus.
Then, for sixteen years,
they shall abandon their lives once Kṛṣṇa has attained his dark dissolution.
In the fifth or even the sixth year, a girl gives birth;
she may be seven or eight years old.
At that time, men will procreate who possess little wealth, who bear false emblems,
who are takers rather than givers.
In the Kali age, men will become base; they will be intent on giving away their own white (pure) wealth,
while the twice-born will subsist on the food of others.
Likewise, Vaiśyas and kings [are not eligible],
nor those born of the Kṣatriya lineage; Śūdras and mendicant Brāhmaṇas [are likewise excluded].
O best of kings,
when Kṛṣṇa has attained his dark dissolution, there will be no disciple and no teacher whatsoever.
O King, in that tumultuous conflict, there will be neither son nor father, neither wife nor husband.
O Śatānīka, best of men, this true nature of time has been declared to you by me for the sake of those devoted to Viṣṇu.
The Kali age does not afflict those men who, day and night, chant the praises of Vāsudeva, the sustainer of the world.
O tiger among men, Kali does not afflict those men who remain with their minds fixed upon them.
O tiger among men, Kali does not afflict those who are setting out, those who are standing still, or those who are sleeping.
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, Govinda, Keśava, and Hari are everywhere; O King, he whose mind is not fixed upon Him [is lost].
Sometimes Kali may cause affliction; yet he does not act like Kali during the Kali age,
nor does he become deluded among the deluded.
He who has constantly surrendered his being to the Blessed One, the Immovable, is not affected by the power of the Kali age or by wicked speech.
The doctrines of the heretics do not affect the mind of him in whose heart Keśava dwells.
For him in whom Govinda dwells in his heart, the Kṛta Age prevails even in the Kali Age; for him, the Kali Age prevails even in the Kṛta Age.
He in whose heart Acyuta does not reside— whether he has not performed great sacrifices or has not offered the *svadhā* oblation to his ancestors— [is lost].
Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa with devotion, the fear of death tomorrow shall not torment him,
whether he stands before Him or behind Him.
Whether walking or standing still,
his mind is fixed upon Govinda;
he is always one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
Having understood this, O protector of the earth,
direct your mind and fix your heart upon Hari, the Lord of all.
With his mind fixed on that, he does not despair;
[he attains] the supreme goal of the entire world, which is the source and the imperishable.
Going for refuge to Govinda, the one worthy of refuge, he does not perish;
[he attains] the imperishable state of Nirvana.
Meditating upon Viṣṇu, the unmanifest cause of all, one does not perish;
for when He who consists of everything is meditated upon, [all is attained].
I bow to Him in whom no other object of meditation exists, and by whose worship He who is worthy of worship is born.
The creator of the world, the Lord of lords, without beginning, higher than the highest,
the abode of all, and the essence of all beings.
He who goes with his whole soul toward Hari removes all sin without exception—
he who is thus celebrated as "Hari."
Salutations to Viṣṇu, the remover of all sins without exception, the golden-hued Hari;
by whose glorification one is purified of sin.
O King, bow to that lotus-eyed one who, when remembered, makes the impure pure and dwells within the self.
Whether impure or pure, or even in whatever state one may be, whoever remembers the lotus-eyed Lord [is purified].
He is pure both internally and externally, even if he has been afflicted by sins or by the most extreme misdeeds.
Nevertheless, by remembering Viṣṇu, he remains pure both internally and externally,
even in this age (yuga) that is so full of faults.
Even after committing a sin, one is liberated from sins by meditating on Govinda;
that meditation is wherein Govinda resides.
That is true discourse wherein Keśava appears;
that is true action which is for His sake. What is the use of many other words?
O King, neither a father would tell his son, nor a teacher his disciple, this supreme state of ultimate reality.
O son, all this that I have spoken to you—
which is obtained by one wandering in *saṃsāra*—
consists of sons, wives, wealth, and possessions.
O King, neither friends nor others can provide such instruction as this; what use are sons, wives, or wealth?
Neither friends nor field-kinsmen are superior;
the truest kinsman is the teacher who leads one to liberation.
O King, he who, even though knowing this, does not have a one-pointed mind toward Viṣṇu,
is surely [the enemy] of Acyuta himself.
In this world, the evildoer is not to be favored.
This creation of beings is of two kinds:
the divine and the demonic.
One who is devoted to Viṣṇu is divine;
one who is the opposite is asuric.
The threefold origin belongs to the asuras.
O King, one whose impurities are not exhausted does not become devoted to Viṣṇu,
even though he is excessively intent upon the instructions.
Aggressive, relying on fallacious reasoning and based on mere sophistry, the fool gives an inexhaustible answer.
For one who has bathed, even a mere portion of that [merit] pertains to rites for the gods, as well as in times of distress and during discourses.
"O King, such an understanding arises. Thinking thus, he spoke this supreme secret concerning the highest state of being.
O King, you must by no means withdraw your mind from Acyuta;
for without attaining him, one finds no true delight.
If the mind of men is always [unstable], why then is it abandoned?
Therefore, enough of this kingdom for you!
Just as one might contemplate with the strength of one's treasury and other resources, so too should Acyuta be contemplated;
for what is destined to be cannot be otherwise.
This is purifying, health-giving, auspicious, and a destroyer of bad dreams; it brings happiness and joy to men.
It bestows liberation upon those who fall [into distress],
and it shall remain eternally in the houses of those in whom it is written.
No calamities arising from fate shall afflict their homes;
for what need have they for sacred fords or for acts of charity?
What is the use of sacrifices or fasts for one who listens to this very thing day after day with a mind absorbed in it?
He who gives a prastha of sesame seeds and a māsaka of gold, and he who hears even a single verse— [these two obtain equal merit].
For this dharma, that [gift] is indeed equal; however,
the completion of this chapter is distinguished by the gift of a cow.
By hearing its ten chapters,
one is immediately liberated from sins; whatever offense one commits during the night, [one is freed from it].
And by means of this day, O Mānava,
that desire of the king to hear it all is dispelled.
O lord of men, that merit which would accrue from giving a hundred tawny cows at Jyeṣṭhapuṣkara belongs to those who follow the dharma of Viṣṇu.
O best among the upholders of dharma, he thereby attains the merit of both the path of worldly engagement and the path of renunciation at the time of breaking his fast.
There is no other supreme scripture equal to the Viṣṇudharmas;
it produces friendliness toward all beings.
Having heard these teachings on dharma, one who possesses supreme devotion to Acyuta understands the world as non-different from the Self.
O best among the wise, by reciting these teachings daily, or likewise by listening to them with devotion, Vdha 105.094.
One is liberated from all sins; there shall be no calamity, no misfortune,
and no fear of thieves or fire in the home.
O protector of the earth, wherever this book remains,
there is no fear of being taken into the womb [by a malevolent spirit].
O Lord of the Earth, in that house where this [mantra] resides, there are no seizing spirits of children,
nor is there any fear of piśācas and the like.
By hearing this, a Brahmin becomes a knower of the Vedas,
a Kṣatriya becomes a lord of the earth, and a Vaiśya attains prosperity.
And a Śūdra attains health; and whoever, endowed with faith, recites these prescribed duties, [attains the same].
Having fully absorbed the mind in Viṣṇu and seeing with equanimity everywhere, his sins as well as his diseases [are destroyed].
And whatever other evil there may be, Keśava destroys it all for one who observes these duties during the winter season.
O Lord of the Earth, he who hears this with perfect faith shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
And in the cool season, O tiger among men,
he who hears [this] according to the rule regarding the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice—
That man obtains the fruit [of his merit] during the months known as Madhu and Mādhava,
he who listens to these [accounts].
O King, he who listens to these [stories] during the summer heat attains the complete fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
O best among the upholders of dharma,
one undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
O lord of the earth, he who listens to these teachings during the rainy season obtains the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
O bull among men, by listening to these dharmas during the autumn season, one shall obtain everything in its entirety.
One who is endowed with perfect faith obtains the fruit of the Gosava sacrifice during these very seasons. Vdha 105.105–106.
O King, even for those who merely recite this,
there is fruit when the planets are malignant; these [mantras] bestow auspiciousness.
Whatever fruit is said to come from giving a hundred tawny cows at Jyeṣṭhapuṣkara,
one obtains that even more and yet more.
Whoever recites these with devotion before the Lord Hari at every conclusion of a fast, Vdha_105.107–Vdha_105.108.
O protector of the earth,
he worships Keśava with the sacrifice of knowledge; thus,
all afflictions as well as sin are destroyed.
O lord of men, the religious duties of Viṣṇu, when remembered, recited, or heard, dispel everything entirely.
All this supreme secret of Hari has been told to you;
there is nothing higher than this.
It is pleasant to hear and brings delight to the ear; for a wise man, O tiger among men, nothing is difficult to attain.
The supreme, eternal Brahman.
